# Compounding Pressures and Scaling Limits {#sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales}

::: {.epigraph}
> "[F]eedback is a method of controlling a system by reinserting into it the results of its past performance. If these results are merely used as numerical data for the criticism of the system and its regulation, we have the simple feedback of the control engineers."
>
> — Norbert Wiener, *The Human Use of Human Beings*, revised edition [@Wiener1989HumanUse, p. 61]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *Why has system and chip design become harder to carry through, and where might AI assistance be useful?*

**Core thesis:** *Compounding pressures across physical scaling, specialization, software co-evolution, and verification demand new abstractions, but assistance helps only when it targets the work that actually limits the next design decision.*
:::

For decades, architects rode the compounding dividends of Dennard scaling and Moore's Law, where shrinking transistors switched faster and packed more tightly while power density remained flat. Once that combined dividend ran out, subthreshold leakage stalled supply-voltage scaling, wire resistance limited signal propagation within a single clock cycle, and thermal budgets left substantial fractions of a die unpowered or throttled. Although architects have turned to specialization by deploying dedicated matrix engines in GPUs and neural processing units (NPUs) to sustain throughput gains, specialization couples decisions across the hardware–software stack until the number of plausible alternatives outgrows the engineering capacity available to evaluate them.

This chapter traces that chain of pressures from subthreshold leakage and interconnect resistance-capacitance (RC) delay to dark silicon, accelerator offload overhead, and rising verification costs. A vast design space is not by itself the problem; what slows a team down is the cost of evaluating candidates inside it. Machine-assisted exploration therefore delivers value only when it relieves the specific bottleneck delaying the next design decision (@fig-ch02-cover-map).

![**Compounding pressures shift the architectural bottleneck.** Fading automatic technology gains, coupled design obligations across hardware and software, and finite simulation and verification capacity converge to limit design velocity. AI assistance helps most when it targets the specific engineering work delaying the next supported decision.](images/ch02-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch02-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which fading technology gains, coupled design obligations, and finite checking capacity converge on the work limiting the next supported decision."}

Because these pressures fall unevenly across projects, the limiting bottleneck shifts from one study to the next. Simulation throughput restricts one design team, while software runtime maturity, missing physical collateral, or formal verification capacity holds back another. Tracing where engineering effort actually concentrates lets an architect identify the work that blocks the next decision and judge whether learned methods or conventional automation will relieve it better, because architectural complexity by itself does not justify applying AI.

## Where Engineering Time Goes in Modern Chip Design

The moonshot in @sec-moonshot asks whether an AI-native design system can make exploring thousands of hardware–software alternatives practical. What makes that exploration expensive is already visible in a familiar design choice. When an architect considers expanding an on-chip Level-2 (L2) cache to relieve memory bandwidth pressure, a capacity-focused simulation may favor the larger cache because it reduces misses. In silicon, however, the additional static random-access memory (SRAM) bitcells consume die area, lengthen interconnects,[^fn-rc-delay-c02] and increase leakage current. Within the thermal envelope of a passively cooled mobile device, that extra leakage reduces the power budget left for the compute cores, so a simulated drop in cache misses answers only part of the architectural question.

[^fn-rc-delay-c02]: **Interconnect scaling and wire delay**: While transistor switching delays decrease as gate lengths shrink, wire delay scales unfavorably. As interconnect cross-sectional dimensions narrow at advanced process nodes, wire resistance ($R$) rises sharply while parasitic capacitance ($C$) plateaus due to fringing fields between densely packed lines. Consequently, distributed $RC$ wire delay across long global lines increasingly dominates cycle times, making large contiguous structures (such as wide cache arrays or cross-chip buses) physically impractical to access within a single clock cycle.

Software offers another way to attack the same memory bottleneck. Loop tiling can shrink the working set until it fits inside a smaller on-chip buffer, at the cost of extra transfer coordination, direct memory access descriptors, and loop-tail control overhead. Weighing a larger L2 cache against a tiled software schedule requires both an executable schedule and characterized physical memory macros. The architect has to decide which hardware–software pairs are worth testing and which measurements will separate them.

Earlier jumps in abstraction kept this kind of design complexity manageable by hiding lower-level detail behind automated tools. Register-transfer level (RTL) descriptions let engineers specify synchronous circuit behavior without placing individual gates by hand.[^fn-rtl-c02] Logic synthesis and place-and-route tools then generated the gate-level layout, while formal equivalence checking and static timing analysis verified functional correctness and path delays. As @sec-moonshot showed, those abstractions succeeded because trustworthy verification tools checked the lower-level implementation automatically. Today's cross-layer, specialized architectures strain that model because hardware and software choices interact across the boundary, forcing many more coupled candidates through those slow implementation and signoff tools.

[^fn-rtl-c02]: **RTL as an architectural contract**: RTL descriptions specify exact cycle-by-cycle state transfers between synchronous registers. While RTL serves as the legal contract for logic synthesis, equivalence checking, and timing signoff, its rigid binding of pipeline stages and clock domains makes automated architectural exploration challenging because modifying a datapath's latency or decoupling an interface often requires restructuring the entire RTL description rather than tuning a high-level parameter.

Each pass through those tools traces what we call a *design path*: proposing an architectural change, building the candidate artifacts, running the simulators and physical-design tools, and comparing the measured results. In the cache study, a single design path evaluates two L2 capacities under a representative workload and compares their latency, dynamic energy, and leakage. That path becomes a closed *design loop* when the measured results steer the next experiment, such as when high leakage pushes the architect toward a smaller cache paired with a tiled software schedule. Whereas a fixed parameter sweep only collects measurements across a preset grid, a design loop uses each result to decide what to try next.

Every turn of that loop spends engineering time, electronic design automation (EDA) tool licenses, and human review on inputs that span RTL source, execution traces, timing constraints, and power-intent specifications.[^fn-eda-constraints-c02] Depending on the project, the slowest step may be assembling those candidate files, waiting on physical signoff runs, or diagnosing verification failures. To see why modern designs force so many cross-layer experiments through this loop, we start with the breakdown of classical transistor and wire scaling.

[^fn-eda-constraints-c02]: **EDA constraint formats**: Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) and Unified Power Format (UPF) describe timing requirements and power intent for EDA tools. Implementation and verification tools use those declarations to check the design under the specified conditions.

## The End of Free Scaling and the Push Toward Specialization {#sec-fracturing-technology-dividend}

For roughly thirty years, processor performance advanced under classical Dennard scaling, where shrinking physical device dimensions reduced transistor area and gate delay while voltage scaling allowed more transistors to switch faster without increasing power density (@tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison) [@Moore1965Cramming; @DennardEtAl1974Scaling; @HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. Today, device technology still supplies transistor density, but it no longer delivers proportional gains in frequency, single-thread performance, or energy efficiency. To extract more performance, architects now have to make choices that tightly bind microarchitecture, software mapping, and physical implementation together.

### The Collapse of Dennard Scaling and the Shift to Specialization

To see why specialization became so attractive, consider the balance in the original scaling model. Classical Dennard scaling assumed that shrinking linear dimensions by a factor $\kappa > 1$ reduced transistor area by $1/\kappa^2$, gate capacitance by $1/\kappa$, supply voltage by $1/\kappa$, and switching delay by $1/\kappa$. With switching activity held constant, $P_{\mathrm{dyn}} = \alpha C V_{dd}^{2} f$ then scaled by $(1/\kappa)(1/\kappa^2)(\kappa)=1/\kappa^2$ per transistor. This reduction exactly counteracted the $\kappa^2$ increase in transistor density and kept dynamic power density constant.

The post-Dennard column in @tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison uses one deliberately simplified assumption set to isolate what changes when voltage and frequency scaling stop: transistor area continues to shrink by $1/\kappa^2$, gate capacitance per transistor falls by $1/\kappa$, and transistor density rises by $\kappa^2$, while activity factor $\alpha$, supply voltage $V_{dd}$, and operating frequency $f$ remain fixed. The dynamic-power calculation excludes leakage and interconnect capacitance, which do not obey this ideal active-device model.

| Device Parameter | Classical Dennard Scaling ($\kappa > 1$) | Simplified Post-Dennard Case | Limiting Physical Constraint |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Transistor Area ($W \times L$)** | $1/\kappa^2$ | $1/\kappa^2$ | Gate pitch scaling continues |
| **Supply Voltage ($V_{dd}$)** | $1/\kappa$ | $1$ *(held fixed)* | Leakage and switching-speed trade-off |
| **Gate Capacitance ($C_{\text{gate}}$)** | $1/\kappa$ | $1/\kappa$ *(idealized)* | Gate and interconnect capacitance scale differently |
| **Operating Frequency ($f$)** | $\kappa$ | $1$ *(held fixed)* | Thermal dissipation and leakage limit frequency gains |
| **Dynamic Power Density ($P_{\mathrm{dyn}} / A$)** | $1$ *(constant)* | $\kappa$ *(under stated assumptions)* | Dark silicon and thermal limits |
: **Classical Dennard scaling versus a simplified post-Dennard case.** Shrinking linear dimensions by a factor $\kappa > 1$ historically kept dynamic power density constant while increasing operating frequency. With voltage, frequency, and activity held fixed in the displayed post-Dennard case, dynamic power density rises by $\kappa$; leakage, interconnect, and nonideal geometric scaling make real product behavior implementation-dependent. {#tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison tbl-colwidths="[24,24,28,24]"}

If we write transistor density as $\rho$, the post-Dennard dynamic-power-density ratio follows directly from that assumption set:
$$
\frac{P_{\mathrm{dyn}}'/A'}{P_{\mathrm{dyn}}/A}
= \frac{\alpha'}{\alpha}
  \times \frac{C'}{C}
  \times \left(\frac{V_{dd}'}{V_{dd}}\right)^2
  \times \frac{f'}{f}
  \times \frac{\rho'}{\rho}
= 1 \times \frac{1}{\kappa} \times 1^2 \times 1 \times \kappa^2
= \kappa.
$$
Dynamic power per active transistor therefore falls by $1/\kappa$, but the $\kappa^2$ increase in transistor density raises dynamic power per unit area by $\kappa$. In physical silicon, static subthreshold leakage, interconnect RC parasitics, nonideal density scaling, and dynamic power management determine how much of that power increase a chip actually experiences.

That classical balance broke down in the mid-2000s because supply voltage could no longer scale down alongside feature size. Lowering supply voltage slows transistor switching unless the threshold voltage also drops, and lowering the threshold voltage drives up off-state leakage exponentially.[^fn-subthreshold-slope-c02] Rather than prescribing a single operating voltage, device physics forces engineers to trade switching speed against active power and leakage. Once voltage reductions stalled, architects could no longer rely on process shrinks alone to deliver simultaneous gains in clock frequency and energy efficiency [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach].

[^fn-subthreshold-slope-c02]: **Subthreshold swing and leakage**: In a conventional thermionic MOS transistor, drain current decreases exponentially as gate voltage falls below threshold. The subthreshold swing is $S = \ln(10) \cdot (k_B T / q) \cdot (1 + C_{\text{dep}} / C_{\text{ox}})$, with an ideal lower limit of approximately $60\ \text{mV/decade}$ at $300\ \text{K}$ under these device assumptions. A threshold reduction $\Delta V_{\text{th}}$ increases off-state current by approximately $10^{\Delta V_{\text{th}}/S}$ if the other parameters remain fixed. The realized swing and allowable leakage depend on the device and operating conditions; the trade-off restricts continued voltage scaling.

Fifty years of microprocessor scaling data from Karl Rupp's CPU sample (1971–2021), joined with a 2012–2026 frontier compiled from the published specifications of twenty-five accelerators including GPUs [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @JouppiEtAl2021TenLessons; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper; @AMD2025CDNA3; @NVIDIA2024B100; @NVIDIA2013K20XBoardSpec; @AMD2021CDNA2; @Myrhang2023AMDInstinctHPC; @Intel2023Gaudi2Datasheet; @Intel2024Gaudi3Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellDatasheet; @NVIDIA2025BlackwellUltraBlog; @NVIDIA2026RubinBlog; @Cerebras2019WSE; @Cerebras2021WSE2; @Cerebras2024WSE3], map this architectural evolution across three eras (@fig-microprocessor-trends). In the *device-scaling era* (1971–2005), single-thread performance, clock frequency, and transistor counts all climbed by orders of magnitude, though at different rates. Around the 2005 Dennard boundary, clock frequency stalled near $3\text{--}5\ \text{GHz}$ in this sample, and single-thread performance growth fell from about 52% per year (1986–2003) to about 23% per year, dropping to single digits by the late 2010s [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. This slowdown ushered in the *parallelism era* (2005–2016), where architects turned to multicore integration and sampled hardware thread counts reached 96 by 2016 and 128 by 2020, while the maximum reported CPU power in each four-year bucket rose from about $200\ \text{W}$ in the mid-2010s to about $290\ \text{W}$ by 2021, where the CPU series ends without establishing a power ceiling for later processors. A third inflection around 2016 marks the *specialization era*, as dedicated datapaths became an increasingly important use of growing transistor budgets.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The readable stacked plot was deferred several pages under top-only placement. -->
![**Frequency scaling slows as transistor budgets and accelerator power ratings grow.** Four-year maxima from Rupp's CPU sample (1971–2021) [@Rupp2022MicroprocessorTrendData] join running maxima from twenty-five accelerators (2012–2026). Accelerator counts reach 336 billion transistors (4 trillion for wafer-scale parts), and power ratings reach $1{,}400\ \text{W}$. Ratings mix thermal design power, board-power limits, and total graphics power, not measured workload power. The CPU series establishes no later power ceiling. Accelerator sources and six dated design reports appear in the text; the hatched band after 2026 marks the emerging AI-native design frontier rather than a fourth measured trend.](images/fig-microprocessor-trends){#fig-microprocessor-trends width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Log-scale chart with CPU sample maxima ending in 2021 and accelerator specification frontiers extending to 2026. CPU frequency growth slows after 2005, while transistor counts and accelerator power ratings increase. A hatched band after 2026 marks a hypothesized AI-native design era; a separate rail dates six AI-assisted design reports."}

The divergence of these curves after 2005 reflects the *dark silicon* limit [@Sutter2005FreeLunch; @EsmaeilzadehEtAl2011DarkSilicon].[^fn-dark-silicon-c02] Once supply voltage stopped scaling, thermal budgets capped the fraction of a chip's transistors that could switch simultaneously at full clock frequency. Duplicating general-purpose cores during the parallelism era converted extra transistors into thread-level concurrency, but serial code sections and shared-memory traffic soon limited the return on adding more homogeneous cores.

Specialization answers that limit by spending the transistor and power budget on dedicated datapaths. Packaged accelerator transistor counts climb from 15.3 billion in the NVIDIA Tesla P100 (2016) to 208 billion in the dual-die Blackwell B200 (2024) and 336 billion in NVIDIA's Rubin GPU (2026), while Cerebras integrates 4 trillion transistors on a single wafer-scale die. Over the same span, published accelerator power ratings rise from the P100's $300\ \text{W}$ thermal design power (TDP) to as much as $1{,}400\ \text{W}$ total graphics power in the Blackwell Ultra generation (2025). Although these ratings describe nominal hardware envelopes rather than measured application efficiency, they show why the industry has directed its silicon budget into regular matrix and tensor arrays that amortize instruction fetch and decode across hundreds of arithmetic units, trading clock-rate scaling for dense spatial parallelism and local data reuse.

The hatched band at the right of @fig-microprocessor-trends asks what comes next. Each earlier era found a new lever when the previous one flattened: device scaling, then parallelism, then specialization. One candidate for the next lever is the design process itself, because the engineering cost and schedule required to build and verify a specialized chip now limit how many architectures a team can attempt. Point deployments have already entered production workflows, starting with learned macro placement for the floorplans of Google's commercial accelerators in 2021 [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement] and a domain-adapted language model trained on internal chip-design data in 2023 [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo]. By 2026, autonomous workflows had synthesized a RISC-V CPU and an inference accelerator [@Verkor2026DesignConductor; @Verkor2026DesignConductor2], Google reported incorporating an AlphaEvolve-proposed circuit into next-generation Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) silicon [@DeepMind2026AlphaEvolveImpact], and OpenAI reported AI assistance across the design of its Jalapeño accelerator [@OpenAI2026JalapenoFirstResults]. Because these early reports focus on individual blocks or design steps rather than comparing total project schedule and engineering cost against an equally tuned conventional team on the same chip, whether AI-native design loops can bend the project-level cost and schedule curve remains the central open question that the rest of this book investigates.

[^fn-dark-silicon-c02]: **Dark silicon**: Silicon that cannot all operate concurrently at full performance within the available power and thermal budget. Power gating, clock gating, and reduced operating rates are among the ways a design manages that limit.

### Diminishing Returns Inside General-Purpose Cores

General-purpose processors continue to improve through branch prediction, speculative execution, wider issue, and better memory hierarchies. These mechanisms can expose and exploit more instruction-level parallelism, but their benefits must pay for the structures needed to coordinate that work.

The out-of-order issue window illustrates this coordination cost. Adding window entries lets a core look farther ahead for independent instructions, and widening issue lets it dispatch more of them per cycle, but every completing instruction must broadcast its result tag to the waiting entries before selection logic chooses which ready instructions fire next. Enlarging the window increases the capacitive load on the content-addressable memory (CAM) tag broadcast lines, while widening issue adds comparators, arbiter priority trees, and bypass forwarding paths (even though a quadratic connection count does not by itself imply a quadratic delay law). The circuit analysis of @PalacharlaEtAl1997ComplexityEffective shows how wakeup, selection, and bypass delays limit the return on wider issue widths,[^fn-palacharla-circuits-c02] and on-chip wire delay further restricts how far signals can travel within a single clock cycle [@AgarwalEtAl2000ClockRateVersusIPC].

[^fn-palacharla-circuits-c02]: **Issue-window circuit limits**: In an out-of-order superscalar core with issue window capacity $W$ and issue width $I$, the wakeup logic broadcasts $I$ result tags across all $W$ waiting instructions every cycle, requiring $I \times W$ CAM comparators whose wire loading scales with window size. Ready instructions then feed selection logic, which uses priority arbiter trees whose gate delay grows with $\log W$ and whose layout routing introduces heavy wire capacitance. In deep-submicron processes, the physical wire delay across these densely routed CAM and arbiter structures, combined with the $O(I^2)$ forwarding paths of the bypass network, raises the cycle-time cost of each further increase in issue width, which is why wide machines partition or cluster these structures [@PalacharlaEtAl1997ComplexityEffective].

Deepening the pipeline runs into a similar limit, as Intel's 31-stage Prescott core demonstrated [@BoggsEtAl2004Pentium4NinetyNm]. Slicing logic into finer stages can raise clock frequency, but every branch misprediction flushes more in-flight instructions and takes more cycles to drain and refill, so a higher clock rate alone does not guarantee shorter runtime or lower energy. Replicating cores on a die shifts the bottleneck again toward cache coherence, memory ordering, synchronization, and workload partitioning. General-purpose microarchitectures continue to advance, but these coordination costs explain why architects increasingly spend new transistors on specialized datapaths instead.

### The Shift to Domain-Specific Accelerators

When a workload performs regular, predictable calculations, a specialized datapath can strip away most of that per-instruction coordination hardware and devote the silicon to dense arithmetic arrays, provided the memory system can keep those units fed.

Across five NVIDIA GPU generations from Pascal P100 (2016) to Blackwell B200 (2024), peak dense half-precision floating-point (FP16) throughput grew by $106\times$ ($21.2\text{ to }2{,}250\ \text{TFLOPS}$), outpacing the $10.9\times$ growth in off-chip High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) supply ($732\text{ to }8{,}000\ \text{GB/s}$) by roughly an order of magnitude while TDP rose $3.3\times$ ($300\text{ to }1{,}000\ \text{W}$) (@fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier a). With precision held fixed and excluding structured sparsity,[^fn-structured-sparsity-c02] this divergence reflects an architectural pivot from P100's conventional vector units to dedicated matrix Tensor Cores across successive process nodes and dual-reticle packaging [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellTechBrief].

[^fn-structured-sparsity-c02]: **Structured vs. unstructured sparsity**: Mathematical weight pruning sets near-zero parameters to zero, but arbitrary (unstructured) sparse matrices introduce irregular memory indexing and load imbalance that frequently degrade performance on parallel vector and matrix hardware. In contrast, hardware-supported structured sparsity (such as NVIDIA's 2:4 pattern introduced in the Ampere architecture) enforces that exactly two out of every four contiguous values in a matrix must be zero. This fixed structural constraint allows dedicated multiplexing hardware to compress storage by $2\times$ and double dense matrix math throughput without the runtime overhead of sparse graph traversal.

Because arithmetic capacity expanded far faster than off-chip memory bandwidth, feeding these datapaths demands much higher data reuse inside the package. If we define a workload's *operational intensity* as the arithmetic operations executed per byte transferred across the HBM boundary, dividing peak compute rate by memory bandwidth gives the off-chip balance point plotted in @fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier b. That dense FP16 balance point escalates tenfold from $29\ \text{FLOP/byte}$ on P100 to $295\ \text{FLOP/byte}$ on H100, before plateauing at $281\ \text{FLOP/byte}$ on B200 as eight-stack HBM3e bandwidth ($8\ \text{TB/s}$) keeps pace with the $2.3\times$ step in dense FP16 compute (while B200's narrower 8-bit and 4-bit floating-point [FP8 and FP4] Tensor Core modes push the required reuse another $2\times\text{ to }4\times$ higher). A kernel operating below its target precision's balance point cannot saturate the matrix engines even with zero control stalls; it remains bandwidth-bound until on-chip buffering or wider memory interfaces shift the ratio.

![**Arithmetic scaling outpaces off-chip memory bandwidth.** (a) Growth relative to P100 in dense FP16 peak throughput, HBM bandwidth, and TDP across five GPU generations from P100 to B200 (2016–2024). (b) The dense FP16 off-chip balance point rises from 29\ FLOP/byte on P100 to 295\ FLOP/byte on H100 and 281\ FLOP/byte on B200, demanding steep operational intensity to saturate peak arithmetic. Hardware specifications exclude structured sparsity [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @NVIDIA2016P100Datasheet; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper; @NVIDIA2022H100Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellTechBrief; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellDatasheet].](images/fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier){#fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel chart for P100, V100, A100, H100, and B200 GPUs from 2016 to 2024. First panel shows dense FP16 peak throughput growing 106 times relative to P100 while HBM bandwidth grows 10.9 times and TDP grows 3.3 times. Second panel shows the dense FP16 off-chip balance point rising from 29 floating-point operations per byte transferred from HBM on P100 to 295 on H100 and 281 on B200."}

### Why Accelerators Coupled the Hardware and Software Stacks

This divergence between arithmetic density and memory supply erodes the classical separation of concerns inside an accelerator design. Where a conventional processor stack lets compiler writers, microarchitects, and process engineers work against relatively independent interfaces, @fig-tao-vs-taos contrasts that modular hierarchy with the coupled regime of domain-specific hardware, in which a single power, thermal, and area envelope ties all three layers together.

![**Specialization makes cross-layer dependencies explicit.** (a) A classical layered view separates optimization, architecture, and technology into modular tiers. (b) The specialization-coupled view reveals how domain specialization binds software mapping, microarchitecture, and silicon fabrication across shared power, thermal, and area constraints.](images/fig-tao-vs-taos){#fig-tao-vs-taos width="80%" fig-alt="Two side-by-side stack diagrams. The first panel shows optimization, architecture, and technology stacked in a top-down hierarchy. The second panel introduces a specialization block coupled across all three tiers, bounded by a shared thermal, power, and area constraint perimeter."}

Specialization does not invent cross-layer coupling, but it removes the slack that once hid it. When an architect chooses a systolic or tensor-core array geometry, that choice fixes which dataflows keep operands local; sizing the on-chip scratchpad to sustain that reuse dictates die area and wire reach; and those physical layout choices determine clock frequency and leakage in the chosen process node. An architectural model that evaluates datapath throughput without accounting for on-chip storage area and physical wire delay will systematically misrank candidates inside the block.

## Balancing Specialization and System Composition

Whereas @sec-fracturing-technology-dividend examined why physical scaling limits push transistor budgets into specialized datapaths inside a chip, a specialized engine delivers end-to-end value only inside the larger system that feeds its inputs and consumes its outputs. Once a custom block is integrated alongside a host processor, a memory hierarchy, and package or wafer interconnects, three system-level composition bounds govern how much of its peak throughput survives: the unaccelerated serial work remaining on the host (Amdahl's law), the latency and bandwidth overhead of offloading work across a link (the LogCA bound), and the physical constraints of multi-die or wafer-scale packaging.

### Specialization Traps and Amdahl's Law

Taking a specialized block's peak operations-per-watt rating at face value is a classic architectural trap because an order-of-magnitude kernel speedup on paper can collapse at the system level when the block accelerates only a narrow slice of the application or stalls waiting on host offload transfers. Even so, the underlying block-level efficiency gains are large enough to pull architects across a continuous spectrum that runs from general-purpose cores with vector extensions to GPUs, programmable domain-specific accelerators, and fixed-function application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs). Narrower specialization trades workload breadth for higher throughput density and energy efficiency. For the H.264 video encoder studied by @HameedEtAl2010Inefficiency, replacing a four-core chip multiprocessor with a fixed-function ASIC improved kernel energy efficiency roughly 500-fold by eliminating instruction fetch and decode overhead and fusing operator pipelines. How much of that block-level gain survives in deployment depends on the surrounding system envelope, from milliwatts and joules per frame in a mobile system-on-chip (SoC) to total cost of ownership and throughput per kilowatt in a data center.

This search for specialized efficiency has produced a remarkably diverse hardware ecosystem, a shift the Project Brainwave team characterized as rapid architectural diversification [@ChungEtAl2018Brainwave]. Rather than converging on a single canonical accelerator template, publicly announced AI chips, cards, and systems spread across the power–performance plane from milliwatt edge devices to multi-kilowatt data-center platforms (@fig-accelerator-landscape) [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS].

```{python}
#| label: fig-accelerator-landscape

Chips are circles, cards squares, and systems triangles; training parts are filled and inference parts hollow."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style
from _python.labels import place_labels

apply_style()

# Data: MIT Lincoln Laboratory AI accelerator survey, 2025 edition
# [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS], one row per publicly announced accelerator with a
# stated peak performance and power. Values are dataset-transcribed.
# Accessed 2026-07-19. Source data: data/datasets/chapter1-accelerator-landscape.csv

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
rows = []
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter1-accelerator-landscape.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    # datasets carry '#' provenance headers; skip them
    for d in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")):
        try:
            perf = float(d["peak_performance_ops_per_s"]) / 1e9
            power = float(d["power_w"])
        except ValueError:
            continue
        rows.append({"label": d["label"], "perf": perf, "power": power,
                     "form": d["form_factor"], "iort": d["inference_or_training"]})

forms = {"Chip": COLORS["workload"], "Card": COLORS["methods"], "System": COLORS["evidence"]}
markers = {"Chip": "o", "Card": "s", "System": "^"}  # shape as well as hue
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.0))
xline = np.array([1e-3, 1e5])
for eff, lab in [(1e2, "100 GOPS/W"), (1e3, "1 TOPS/W"), (1e4, "10 TOPS/W"), (1e5, "100 TOPS/W")]:
    ax.plot(xline, eff * xline, ls=(0, (5, 4)), color=COLORS["grid"], lw=0.8, zorder=1)
    x_pos = max(2.4e-3, 10.0 / eff)
    ax.text(x_pos, eff * x_pos * 1.3, lab, fontsize=4.6, color=COLORS["muted"],
            rotation=34, rotation_mode="anchor", va="bottom", ha="left", zorder=1)
for form, color in forms.items():
    for iort, filled in [("training", True), ("inference", False)]:
        pts = [d for d in rows if d["form"] == form and d["iort"] == iort]
        if not pts:
            continue
        xs = [d["power"] for d in pts]
        ys = [d["perf"] for d in pts]
        if filled:
            ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=14, marker=markers[form], facecolor=color, edgecolor=color, linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.9, zorder=3)
        else:
            ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=14, marker=markers[form], facecolors="white", edgecolors=color, linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.95, zorder=3)
for txt, x, y in [("Very low power", 0.02, 3.0e3), ("Embedded / autonomous", 3.0, 1.2e1),
                  ("Data-center cards", 5e1, 2.5e6), ("Data-center systems", 1.5e4, 2.5e5)]:
    ax.text(x, y, txt, fontsize=5.2, fontstyle="italic", color=COLORS["muted"], ha="center", va="center", zorder=2)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(8e-4, 7e4)
ax.set_ylim(3, 1e8)
ax.set_xlabel("Peak power (W)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("Peak performance (GOps/sec)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.2, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _sp in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_sp].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
handles = [Line2D([0], [0], marker=markers[f], ls="", markerfacecolor=c, markeredgecolor=c, markersize=5, label=f) for f, c in forms.items()]
handles += [Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor=COLORS["ink"], markeredgecolor=COLORS["ink"], markersize=5, label="Training"),
            Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor="white", markeredgecolor=COLORS["ink"], markersize=5, label="Inference")]
ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=5.8, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3, borderaxespad=0.4)
curated = ["Maxim", "GAP9", "Jetson1", "Perceive", "A100", "TPU4", "H100",
           "AMD-MI300X", "B200", "Gaudi3", "CS-2", "DGX-H100", "GroqNode", "Tachyum"]
by_label: dict[str, dict] = {}
for d in rows:
    if d["label"] not in by_label or d["perf"] > by_label[d["label"]]["perf"]:
        by_label[d["label"]] = d
items = [(by_label[n]["power"], by_label[n]["perf"], n) for n in curated if n in by_label]
place_labels(ax, fig, items, fontsize=5.0, color=COLORS["ink"])
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.095, right=0.98, top=0.98, bottom=0.11)
```

The spread in @fig-accelerator-landscape reflects the diversity of deployment targets rather than a single ranking of designs, because the plotted points mix numerical precisions, supported operations, and chip, card, and system boundaries. Where a subwatt sensor processor emphasizes local storage and low-precision arithmetic to avoid costly off-chip transfers, a data-center accelerator devotes orders of magnitude more power to compute arrays and high-bandwidth memory.

Even two accelerators at similar peak power and throughput on that plot can feed their arithmetic units through very different internal organizations. Systolic arrays maximize local operand reuse through fixed register-to-register pipelines, whereas streaming multiprocessors rely on massive multithreading and deep cache hierarchies to hide memory latency. Because each organization places different demands on compiler scheduling, memory access patterns, and runtime invocation, peak datasheet ratings cannot show how a block will perform once embedded in a full system.

In a composed system, a domain-specific accelerator typically handles dense kernels while a general-purpose host core retains control flow and irregular work, leaving the runtime to move data and synchronize execution between them. Before committing die area and power to that specialized block, architects need to know what fraction $f$ of the workload it actually accelerates and how much the host-to-accelerator crossing costs. Amdahl's law makes that first system-level bound explicit (@eq-amdahl-communication):

$$S_{\mathrm{total}} = \frac{1}{(1-f) + \frac{f}{S_{\mathrm{accel}}} + t_{\mathrm{comm}}}$${#eq-amdahl-communication}

where $S_{\mathrm{accel}}$ is the execution speedup on the specialized block and $t_{\mathrm{comm}}$ is the nonoverlapped transfer and synchronization time, normalized to baseline execution time. Even with free communication ($t_{\mathrm{comm}} = 0$), an infinitely fast accelerator cannot deliver more than $1/(1-f)$ total speedup [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor], and any nonoverlapped communication lowers that ceiling further. Just as Amdahl's law bounded end-to-end design-schedule speedups in @sec-moonshot, here it tests whether a faster datapath can pay for its system integration cost.

How tightly that bound pinches depends on whether the problem size can grow with the hardware. Under Gustafson's law, a system scales the parallel work as more processors become available, as a training study might do with a larger model or dataset [@Gustafson1988AmdahlLaw]. Latency-critical workloads face a stricter test because a mobile extended-reality (XR) pipeline has fixed per-frame work and a hard deadline, so dispatch and synchronization consume wall-clock time that extra arithmetic units cannot recover. Evaluating the accelerator therefore requires evaluating the compiler, runtime, memory traffic, and residual host work alongside it.

That judgment can be made quantitative by adapting the LogCA accelerator model of @AltafWood2017LogCA. Whereas Amdahl's $t_{\mathrm{comm}}$ lumps every communication cost into a single normalized term, LogCA characterizes an offload through five parameters: communication latency ($L$), fixed invocation overhead ($o$), offload granularity ($g$, the payload size in work units), computational index ($CI$, work units per byte transferred across the link), and fixed-function acceleration ($A$) [@AltafWood2017LogCA]. We can write the fixed launch and round-trip latency cost as $o$ cycles,[^fn-host-dispatch-overhead-c02] the host execution cost as $C_h$ cycles per work unit, the inverse of LogCA's computational index as $d = 1/CI$ bytes transferred per work unit over a link of bandwidth $B$ bytes per cycle, and the overlapped transfer interval as $T_{\mathrm{overlap}}(g)$ cycles (or, equivalently, express time in nanoseconds, work in FLOPs, and bandwidth in gigabytes per second). The host and accelerator completion times are then:

[^fn-host-dispatch-overhead-c02]: **Mechanics of invocation overhead ($o$)**: Launching work on an off-chip accelerator can involve command-buffer preparation, driver calls, queue submission, and a memory-mapped hardware doorbell. Buffer registration and address mapping may be paid during setup or repeated, depending on the runtime. User-space queues and persistent execution can reduce the work paid per launch. The relevant overhead is the measured cost on the workload's actual invocation path; physical-link latency alone does not determine it.

$$
T_{\mathrm{host}}(g) = C_h g,
\qquad
T_{\mathrm{acc}}(g) = o + \frac{C_h g}{A} + \max\left(0,\frac{d g}{B} - T_{\mathrm{overlap}}(g)\right).
$$

The ratio of these two completion times gives the delivered offload speedup (@eq-logca-speedup-bound):

$$
S(g) = \frac{C_h g}{o + C_h g/A + \max\left(0,\, d g/B - T_{\mathrm{overlap}}(g)\right)}.
$${#eq-logca-speedup-bound}

In the nonoverlapped regime ($T_{\mathrm{overlap}} = 0$), solving $S(g^*) = 1$ gives a closed-form expression for the break-even granularity $g^*$ that a kernel must exceed before offloading achieves net acceleration ($S(g) > 1$):

$$
C_h g = o + \frac{C_h g}{A} + \frac{d g}{B}
\implies
g\left[C_h\left(1 - \frac{1}{A}\right) - \frac{d}{B}\right] = o
$$

which yields

$$
g^* = \frac{o}{C_h\left(1 - \frac{1}{A}\right) - \frac{d}{B}}.
$${#eq-logca-breakeven-g}

For a positive invocation overhead and $A>1$, this break-even granularity exists only when the denominator is positive. If one work unit represents one arithmetic operation, LogCA's computational index $CI = 1/d$ equals the operational intensity $\mathrm{OI}$ of the Roofline model [@Williams2009Roofline]. When operational intensity falls to or below

$$
\mathrm{OI} \le \mathrm{OI}^* = \frac{1}{B \cdot C_h\left(1 - \frac{1}{A}\right)}
$$

the denominator of @eq-logca-breakeven-g becomes nonpositive. At the specified acceleration $A$, transfer takes at least as much time per operation as offloading saves, so no payload size produces a speedup. A faster datapath (larger $A$) lowers $\mathrm{OI}^*$ slightly, but cannot eliminate the per-byte transfer cost. This distinction separates a fixed invocation cost that a larger payload can amortize from a per-operation transfer cost that it cannot.

Those two terms call for different architectural remedies. Lowering invocation overhead $o$ shrinks the payload needed to amortize each launch, whereas relaxing the operational-intensity bound requires either wider link bandwidth $B$ or fewer transferred bytes per operation $d$, since enlarging the payload alone cannot help when data movement grows in proportion to work.

To apply @eq-logca-breakeven-g to a real machine, an architect must measure the actual invocation path, achieved transfer rate, host execution cost, and accelerator execution time rather than reading a link specification in isolation, because driver calls, runtime queues, synchronization, and bus protocols all shape the costs a workload pays. An empirical sweep of end-to-end execution time across payload sizes tests whether the predicted crossover occurs and how much transfer overlap shifts it. Even after startup overhead is amortized, nonoverlapped transfers still cap asymptotic speedup below the local compute factor $A$, which serves only as an upper bound approached when communication costs vanish; estimating that gap requires modeling a plausible invocation path alongside the datapath itself.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{18\baselineskip}
```

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The unamortized offload wall"}
**The trap.** A team treats the local matrix-multiply acceleration of an NPU as the expected system speedup without measuring dispatch and transfer costs.

**The mechanism.** Invoking the accelerator separately for small layers can leave too little useful work to amortize each launch. Transfer costs add to that penalty. The host baseline also matters, because vectorized execution can reduce host time enough to erase a benefit measured against scalar code. Both $C_h$ and the relative acceleration $A$ must describe that optimized baseline.

**The lesson.** Measure the complete offload against optimized host execution. Layer fusion and kernel batching can increase payload size $g$ and reduce intermediate transfers; a lower-cost submission path can reduce $o$. If feasible changes still leave the offload below break-even, retaining host execution is the supported choice.
:::

While the physical interconnect and invocation path set the baseline transfer and startup costs, the compiler and runtime determine the payload size, data reuse, and communication overlap that the workload actually achieves. This division of responsibility exposes where the operational layers defined in @sec-three-operational-layers reach their limits. A Layer 2 search that tunes array dimensions, buffer capacities, or loop-unroll factors inside a frozen container can alter local acceleration $A$ and, through improved reuse, shrink transferred data $d$, but it cannot modify the invocation path governing $o$ or the physical link governing $B$. At fixed data movement, raising $A$ alone cannot push the break-even threshold $\mathrm{OI}^*$ below $1/(B \cdot C_h)$, whereas reducing $d$ raises achieved operational intensity and may clear the threshold without touching an interface. Before an architect or an exploration study concludes that a system needs a new interface, it must show that feasible reuse and mapping choices inside the existing container cannot reach break-even.

Redesigning the interface itself moves the problem from parameter tuning to cross-layer co-design. Kernel fusion, user-space submission queues, persistent kernels, and custom instruction extensions each alter $o$, $d$, or the payload $g$, and conventional hardware–software co-design teams make those changes routinely today. An AI-native design system (Layer 3) would be permitted to propose such interface changes alongside the hardware parameters, but whether it can do so better or more cheaply than a conventional team remains to be demonstrated. We return to how software stacks shape this offload bound after examining how specialized blocks are packaged into full chips and wafers.

### Packaging and Chiplet Composition Risks

An accelerator that clears its offload threshold in standalone simulation can still fail once integrated into an SoC or multi-chiplet package alongside third-party intellectual property (IP), because die-edge shoreline limits can choke off-die bandwidth, a single defective die can spoil an assembled multi-chiplet package, and undocumented reset or clock-domain assumptions inside encrypted IP can deadlock the system bus. Teams accept these integration hazards because specialized blocks rarely ship in isolation. Partitioning a large design into smaller chiplets can improve manufacturing yield under random-defect models and let different functions use separate process nodes while spreading development cost across products, provided packaging, assembly yield, test, and interconnect overheads do not erase the savings [@Murphy1964CostSize; @FengMa2022ChipletActuary]. Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) standardizes die-to-die physical layers and protocols [@UCIeConsortium2026Spec], yet a standard link neither chooses the partition nor guarantees that a package can supply the required power and shoreline bandwidth.[^fn-shoreline-bandwidth-c02]

[^fn-shoreline-bandwidth-c02]: **Shoreline bandwidth density**: The communication bandwidth available per unit of die edge, often expressed per millimeter. In a side-by-side chiplet arrangement, interface placement, connection pitch, and signaling rate constrain the bandwidth that can cross the available edge.

Opaque third-party blocks compound those physical packaging limits because the system architect cannot inspect their internal implementation. Arm has supplied processor IP as fixed hard macros [@Arm2013CortexA15HardMacro] and Intel distributes encrypted RTL [@Intel2024EncryptedRTLIP], forcing integration to rely on documented behavior, supplied models, and checks at the accessible interfaces. Even when both sides implement a standard bus such as Arm's Advanced eXtensible Interface [@Arm2020AXI], power-sequencing, reset, clock-domain crossing, or coherence behaviors left unspecified at the boundary can make two individually verified blocks fail together. Shared network-on-chip traffic introduces a similar composition hazard when bursty contention across a fabric with adequate average bandwidth causes a latency-critical engine to miss its deadline, while multi-die partitioning requires pre-bond test access so that defective chiplets are screened out before assembly [@IEEE2020Std1838].[^fn-kgd-yield-c02]

[^fn-kgd-yield-c02]: **Known-good die (KGD) and package yield**: For $N$ independently yielding dies, with assembly yield defined conditional on good inputs, a simple model gives $Y_{\text{package}} = Y_{\text{assembly}} \cdot \prod_{i=1}^N Y_{\text{die}, i}$. Without preassembly screening, defects in any constituent die can consume an otherwise usable package. Known-good-die testing reduces that risk by screening chiplets before bonding. Test escapes, correlated defects, and assembly failures remain; screening does not guarantee a functional finished package.

Automated exploration has to account for these integration constraints, because missing rules waste evaluations on physically infeasible combinations while overly restrictive rules prune away viable ones. The Semiconductor Research Corporation (SRC) Microelectronics and Advanced Packaging Technologies (MAPT) roadmap highlights inconsistent supplier data formats, syntax, and semantics as a primary obstacle to cross-vendor automation [@SemiconductorResearchCorporation2023MAPT]. Rather than treating unverified compatibility as silent permission or blanket prohibition, an exploration study needs to encode the interface rules it can verify and flag the remaining assumptions that require integration testing or supplier clarification.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

### Wafer-Scale Communication Trade-offs {#sec-wafer-scale-communication-tradeoffs}

Keeping an entire array of cores and SRAM on an unbroken wafer escapes those die-to-die shoreline and package-assembly bottlenecks, only to confront severe power-delivery, defect-routing, and long-wire communication ceilings [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS; @PalEtAl2019WaferscaleGPU]. Cerebras illustrates both sides of that trade-off with its Wafer-Scale Engine (WSE), which keeps a $46{,}225\text{ mm}^2$ compute and SRAM fabric on one unbroken silicon substrate rather than partitioning it across board-level packages (@fig-cerebras-wse-scale).

![**Wafer-scale integration expands the area available for local computation and storage.** Area-proportional squares compare the first-generation Cerebras WSE's reported $46{,}225\ \text{mm}^2$ with the NVIDIA V100's $815\text{ mm}^2$, a ratio of about 57 [@Cerebras2019WSE; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta]. The squares represent published areas, not mechanical outlines or a wafer-cutting layout. The WSE contains 1.2 trillion transistors, 400,000 cores, and 18\ GB of on-chip SRAM, with communication crossing reticle boundaries. Keeping computation and communication on-wafer reduces reliance on board-level links but requires specialized power delivery, cooling, and defect tolerance.](images/fig-cerebras-wse-scale){#fig-cerebras-wse-scale width="70%" fig-alt="Area comparison diagram in which two separate squares compare the published Cerebras WSE area of 46,225 square millimeters with the NVIDIA V100 die area of 815 square millimeters, a ratio of about 57. The shapes do not represent mechanical chip outlines."}

The WSE's internal SRAM bandwidth describes a different memory boundary from the HBM bandwidth in @fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier and should not be read as a directly interchangeable specification. Although bringing more memory onto the wafer changes which transfers remain local, the benefit depends on how the workload maps onto the distributed storage and compute. In a wafer-scale GPU case study, physical constraints reduced usable capacity from a nominal 100 GPU modules to 40 [@PalEtAl2019WaferscaleGPU], showing why available silicon area is not equivalent to usable compute once placement, routing around defects, and software scheduling determine the communication that the workload actually experiences. Across these packaging choices, the same question persists: can the software use the proposed organization well enough to justify its costs, and what executable software path is required to answer it?

## Workload Volatility and Software–Hardware Coupling

Answering that question requires treating software as part of the architectural evaluation itself, because an optimizing compiler can fuse operations into a payload large enough to clear break-even thresholds while runtime driver traps can add enough dispatch overhead to erase the hardware gain. A credible evaluation therefore needs an executable path to compile, schedule, and drive the candidate hardware, and that path continues to shift after silicon is fixed as software stacks mature and emerging workloads change which hardware features matter. Architects face two distinct challenges: making a specialized mechanism usable at tapeout, and ensuring that it remains useful as software evolves.

### Why Hardware Gains Require a Working Compiler Path

```{=latex}
\suppressfloats[t]
```

A custom matrix unit or instruction extension that looks transformative in a hand-coded microbenchmark will sit idle in production as orphan hardware if no compiler pass, kernel library, or runtime driver can map application graphs onto it without register spills or launch overhead. Avoiding that outcome requires a complete *executable software path* connecting a programming model or front end through the compiler, libraries and kernels, runtime, driver or firmware, and operating-system and deployment controls. Different systems need different combinations of these components, but every candidate requires enough of the path in place for the workload to reach the hardware with its intended behavior and without losing the expected benefit to dispatch overhead or extra data movement, something a peak floating-point operations per second specification alone cannot establish.

One way to organize that work is a *compiler narrow waist*: a shared intermediate representation (IR) through which multiple programming models and hardware targets pass. Common transformations can operate on the IR, while target-specific lowering maps operations onto a particular machine. Halide separates an algorithm from its execution schedule [@RaganKelleyEtAl2017HalideCACM]; Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) provides infrastructure for transformations across levels of abstraction [@LattnerEtAl2020MLIR].[^fn-mlir-c02] Such abstractions can share work across targets, but each target still needs suitable lowering, runtime support, and validation.

[^fn-mlir-c02]: **MLIR dialect ecosystem**: MLIR avoids a monolithic IR by organizing transformations into modular, domain-specific *dialects*. High-level tensor operations (such as linear algebra in the `linalg` dialect) undergo progressive lowering through structured control flow (`scf`) and arithmetic dialects down to low-level hardware representations (`llvm` or vendor-specific GPU dialects like `nvvm`), enabling optimizations to execute at the level of abstraction where domain semantics are most readily preserved.

The software that exposes hardware capabilities has a substantial implementation footprint (@fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall). While CUTLASS's architecture-specific headers contain templates and inline virtual assembly statements for using specialized instructions (@fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall a) [@NVIDIACUTLASS], Triton's selected source trees include a shared compiler, target-specific lowering, runtime interfaces, and vendored headers (@fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall b) [@TilletEtAl2019Triton], and production serving frameworks such as vLLM also contain native kernels (@fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall c) [@KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention]. The measured source trees have grown across the sampled releases, although their line counts combine shared, vendored, and target-specific files rather than isolating porting effort or engineering maintenance hours.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The readable stacked panels and caption were deferred several pages under top-only placement. -->
![**Software source trees document an expanding implementation footprint.** Newline counts measured at release tags show (a) CUTLASS architecture-specific headers reaching about 208,000 lines and inline `asm volatile` statements passing 3,000; (b) Triton's selected trees reaching about 280,000 lines, including vendored headers, examples, and tests; and (c) vLLM native kernels reaching about 120,000 lines [@NVIDIACUTLASS; @TilletEtAl2019Triton; @KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention]. Directory reorganizations limit comparisons of subcategories; these counts do not measure maintenance cost.](images/fig-ch09-software-porting-wall){#fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Three-panel bar chart of source lines at selected release tags. CUTLASS headers grow to about 690 thousand lines, including about 208 thousand architecture-specific lines, and inline assembly statements exceed 3,000. Triton's selected source trees total about 86 thousand lines at v1, fall at v2, and rise to about 280 thousand at v3.7; totals include vendored headers, examples, and tests. vLLM native kernel sources grow to about 120 thousand lines, with a directory reorganization at v0.27."}

For the architect, these growing codebases show that every new hardware mechanism carries a software development and maintenance cost. A matrix instruction needs a lowering path that matches its operand layout, and an asynchronous transfer engine needs scheduling and synchronization that preserve correctness. Shared compilers reduce duplication across targets while hand-tuned libraries expose hardware features before general compilers support them, but both routes must still produce a working binary that the evaluation can run.

Tracing that flow from source code to hardware execution in @fig-codegen-narrow-waist shows where workload structure, architectural mechanisms, and physical constraints meet. Front-end abstract syntax trees first lower into mid-level representations such as MLIR and LLVM IR for target-independent loop and memory optimizations, before target-specific lowering stages map those operations onto machine instructions, accelerator dataflows, and runtime drivers within the chip's power and timing limits.

![**Executable target software paths connect developer intent to verification checks.** High-level domain-specific abstract syntax trees (Python, Triton domain-specific languages) lower through mid-level control-data flow graphs in MLIR dialects and LLVM IR at the compiler narrow waist, where workload intent, architectural mechanisms such as CPU instruction-set extensions and NPU dataflows, and silicon constraints converge. Lowered machine code and runtimes then pass through verification checks for correctness, performance, portability, and maintainability.](images/fig-codegen-narrow-waist){#fig-codegen-narrow-waist width="80%" fig-alt="Diagram of an executable target software path showing programming models, compiler representations, libraries, runtimes, and generated code connecting hardware constraints to correctness, performance, portability, and maintainability checks."}

The break-even bound in @eq-logca-breakeven-g quantifies how much those compiler and runtime choices matter. In the nonoverlapped offload model, acceleration pays off only when operation granularity $g$ exceeds $g^*$ and operational intensity stays above $\mathrm{OI}^*$. Fusing operations in the compiler creates offload payloads large enough to amortize dispatch overhead $o$, while keeping intermediate tensors on chip shrinks the bytes transferred per unit of work $d$ and moves the kernel across the break-even boundary.

Keeping more values live inside a fused kernel, however, increases pressure on the register file during loop scheduling and instruction selection. In scalable vector architectures such as the RISC-V Vector extension, the compiler chooses the active vector length and register group multiplier ($LMUL$) to balance loop-control overhead against register pressure. Setting $LMUL=8$ amortizes instruction issue across wide register groups and processes up to $\text{VLMAX} = LMUL \cdot \text{VLEN} / SEW$ elements per iteration (where $\text{VLEN}$ is the architectural vector register length in bits and $SEW$ is the selected element width in bits), but bundling the 32 architectural vector registers into eight-register groups leaves only four independent groups [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA]. If a fused kernel holds more live values than those four groups can accommodate, registers spill to memory, adding traffic and lowering operational intensity; smaller multipliers such as $LMUL=1$ or $LMUL=2$ preserve 32 or 16 groups to avoid spills at the cost of executing more loop iterations.

Peak vector width alone cannot settle which regime wins. Resolving that trade-off requires running compiled code on the target hardware or simulator with the intended numerics, memory ordering, and application binary interface intact. Whereas an autotuner such as AutoTVM searches compiler schedules on a fixed machine [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM], a joint hardware–software study varies the machine at the same time, so each hardware–schedule pair must be evaluated on equal footing before an apparent speedup can guide a silicon commitment.

Even a thorough evaluation of a compiled workload captures only one point in time. As compilers mature and workloads evolve, both the schedules that run best and the operations that dominate execution can shift while the hardware is still under development.

### Changing Software and Fixed Hardware {#sec-software-changes-faster-than-silicon}

Because a chip takes years to specify, verify, and fabricate, an architectural comparison may need to be revisited before silicon ships even when the RTL itself has not changed. A datapath or memory hierarchy tuned for one model family and compiler release often meets different tensor shapes, kernel schedules, and serving regimes by the time it reaches deployment.

Several software shifts commonly occur during that window, including new key-value (KV) cache allocators,[^fn-kv-cache-fragmentation-c02] fused compiler schedules, and different serving batch sizes. Numerical formats pose an especially sharp commitment problem because supporting FP8, 4-bit integer, or block-scale representations changes the arithmetic units and datapaths built into silicon,[^fn-block-scale-formats-c02] and models may move to a new format after the hardware team has already frozen which data types the array executes natively.

[^fn-kv-cache-fragmentation-c02]: **KV cache scaling and memory fragmentation**: In autoregressive Transformer generation, attention keys and values for previously generated tokens are cached in memory to avoid redundant recomputation. Because sequence lengths grow dynamically by one token at each generation step, allocators that reserve contiguous buffers for a worst-case sequence length (such as 8,192 or 128,000 tokens) cause internal and external fragmentation. @KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention measured that such systems left only 20% to 38% of the memory reserved for KV cache holding actual token state, wasting 60% to 80% of that KV-cache allocation. Their vLLM system introduces paged allocation (PagedAttention) to assign non-contiguous physical blocks dynamically as tokens are generated.

[^fn-block-scale-formats-c02]: **Block-scale formats**: Low-precision number formats amortize shared exponent or scale metadata across a block of elements rather than storing independent metadata for every element [@RouhaniEtAl2023Microscaling]. Committing to one in silicon fixes datapath choices even as formats and workloads continue to evolve, requiring careful judgment of whether the choice will remain useful over time.

Before tapeout, hardware and software teams can still revise the design together, although late RTL changes grow progressively more expensive; after tapeout, only software can adapt the fixed machine to new workloads. Evaluating those updates requires distinguishing a better software implementation of the same task from a change in the task itself. A faster kernel for the original workload can strengthen the case for the existing hardware, whereas a new model shape or accuracy target changes the problem the chip is asked to solve.

Deciding whether such a shift invalidates an earlier hardware choice requires tracking the specific assumptions that specialization built into the design. Because a specialized datapath trades general-purpose flexibility for efficiency and throughput, the architect has to identify which workload properties are stable enough to hardwire into silicon and test when a new workload exceeds the hardware's remaining margin. The six assumption groups in @fig-domain-specificity-shapes span the kernel family, data types and precision, memory behavior, programming interface, deployment quality-of-service targets, and operating conditions. None of these properties needs to stay frozen over the life of the chip, provided the shifts remain within the flexibility the architecture retained.

![**Specialization depends on assumptions about the target workload.** The six groups identify changes that may affect the value of a specialized design. A change calls for checking the affected assumptions; it need not invalidate the design or require repeating every evaluation.](images/fig-domain-specificity-shapes){#fig-domain-specificity-shapes width="80%" fig-alt="Diagram in which six source-to-target conditions surround the specialization scope: kernel family, data and precision, memory behavior, program interface, deployment and quality of service, and operating change. A separate bar states that changes in any condition can increase the verification burden."}

```{python}

ml12_int_tpot = f"{round(_ml12['latency_contract_ms']['interactive_tpot_ms']):,}"
ml12_min_pct = f"{100 * _ml12['minimum_interactive_fraction']:.1f}"
ml12_max_pct = f"{100 * _ml12['maximum_interactive_fraction']:.1f}"
ml12_med_pct = f"{100 * _ml12['median_interactive_fraction']:.1f}"
```

When a workload shift crosses one of those boundaries, earlier efficiency conclusions can fail quickly. An expanded working set that overflows scratchpad capacity triggers costly unmodeled dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) spill traffic, while a smaller serving batch size can shrink the payload per invocation below the break-even threshold $g^*$. Stricter deployment quality-of-service targets cut delivered throughput just as sharply. Across `{python} ml12_pairs` matched single-node, eight-accelerator Llama 2 70B server submissions in MLPerf Inference v5.0 [@MLCommons2025InferenceV50Results], tightening 99th-percentile latency bounds from `{python} ml12_std_ttft`\ ms time to first token and `{python} ml12_std_tpot`\ ms time per output token (Standard) to `{python} ml12_int_ttft`\ ms and `{python} ml12_int_tpot`\ ms (Interactive) restricts interactive server throughput to `{python} ml12_min_pct`% to `{python} ml12_max_pct`% of standard throughput on the same hardware (median `{python} ml12_med_pct`%; @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack examines how that contract change alters transfer and ranking). Even when operational intensity, data reuse, and numerical semantics remain unchanged, shifts in service-level targets, compiler scheduling, synchronization, or runtime overhead can still alter delivered performance, so tracking the assumptions behind a design decision tells the team which measurements an update requires.

Recent AI workloads illustrate how quickly both model structure and compute scale can cross those boundaries. Whereas convolutional inference with fixed frame sizes follows a regular schedule, autoregressive Transformer serving introduces dynamic control and memory behavior through growing KV caches [@KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention], variable sequence lengths, sparse mixture-of-experts routing,[^fn-mixture-of-experts-c02] and separate prefill and decode phases [@AgrawalEtAl2024SarathiServe]. At the same time, the compute scale of frontier models has expanded rapidly. Epoch AI reported a four- to fivefold annual increase in training compute for notable models through May 2024 [@SevillaRoldan2024ComputeGrowth], and an unweighted least-squares fit to a frozen July 2026 snapshot of the same database yields roughly 4.4-fold annual growth across entries that combine published figures with estimates of varying confidence (@fig-training-compute-growth) [@EpochAI2025AIModels]. Larger training runs do not automatically change the underlying kernel mix, but performance measured at one model scale or serving regime does not transfer to another without re-evaluating memory traffic and software assumptions.

[^fn-mixture-of-experts-c02]: **Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing**: A sparsely gated model activates only a subset of its expert subnetworks for each input [@ShazeerEtAl2017MoE]. Because this input-dependent routing forces memory traffic to vary from token to token instead of following one fixed schedule, hardware must be designed to serve highly dynamic memory demands.

```{python}
import csv
import datetime
import math
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]

def _year(text):
    for fmt in ("%Y-%m-%d", "%Y-%m", "%Y"):
        try:
            d = datetime.datetime.strptime(text.strip(), fmt)
            return d.year + (d.timetuple().tm_yday - 1) / 365.25
        except ValueError:
            continue
    return None

pts = []
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-training-compute.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    # datasets carry '#' provenance headers; skip them
    for row in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")):
        yr = _year(row["publication_date"])
        try:
            flop = float(row["training_compute_flop"])
        except ValueError:
            flop = None
        if yr and flop and flop > 0 and 2010 <= yr <= 2026.6:
            pts.append({"yr": yr, "flop": flop, "name": row["model"], "frontier": row["frontier"] == "1"})

years = np.array([p["yr"] for p in pts])
logf = np.array([math.log10(p["flop"]) for p in pts])
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(years, logf, 1)
growth = 10 ** slope

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 3.3))
other = [p for p in pts if not p["frontier"]]
front = [p for p in pts if p["frontier"]]
ax.scatter([p["yr"] for p in other], [p["flop"] for p in other], s=8, marker="o",
           facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6, zorder=2, label="Notable models")
ax.scatter([p["yr"] for p in front], [p["flop"] for p in front], s=12, marker="o",
           facecolor=COLORS["workload"], edgecolor=COLORS["workload_ink"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=3, label="Frontier models")
xline = np.array([2010, 2026.5])
ax.plot(xline, 10 ** (intercept + slope * xline), color=COLORS["constraints"], lw=1.5, zorder=4)
ax.text(2018.0, 10 ** (intercept + slope * 2018.8), f"×{growth:.1f} per year", fontsize=6.6,
        fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"], rotation=29, rotation_mode="anchor",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", alpha=0.9))

by_name = {p["name"]: p for p in pts}
landmarks = {"AlexNet": ("AlexNet", 6, -12), "AlphaGo Zero": ("AlphaGo Zero", -8, 11),
             "GPT-3 175B (davinci)": ("GPT-3", -8, 11), "GPT-4 (Jun 2023)": ("GPT-4", 6, 10)}
for key, (label, dx, dy) in landmarks.items():
```
