Because silicon teams overlap multiple generations in flight and freeze major datapath or packaging choices long before a product is announced, public release intervals do not show when a given hardware decision became expensive to revise. Architects therefore have to judge workload volatility against the lead time and remaining flexibility of the specific mechanism under study, rather than against a generic chip-release interval.

To compare candidate machines while software is moving, architects rely on standardized benchmark suites that hold tasks and run rules fixed for a defined period. Within a single MLPerf version, division, scenario, and accuracy target, the rules allow teams to compare different hardware platforms while still optimizing their own software stacks [@ReddiEtAl2020MLPerfInference]. That comparability comes from actively maintaining the benchmark specification rather than from the models themselves, and it holds only while the tasks and rules remain aligned with deployment.[^fn-metrology-calibration-c02] Once a suite revises its reference models or quality targets, earlier measurements may no longer answer the current design question.

[^fn-metrology-calibration-c02]: **Metrological traceability**: A measurement result is traceable when it can be related to a reference through a documented, unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing uncertainty [@NIST2021MetrologicalTraceability]. While architecture benchmarks do not create this kind of formal calibration chain, explicit versions for tasks, run rules, and measurement procedures remain essential so that reviewers can verify when two results remain genuinely comparable.

Even within a single domain such as mobile XR, an application label is too broad to define that benchmark contract on its own. Sensor fusion, head tracking, and neural rendering impose different latency deadlines and memory-access patterns across the SoC. In our Lighthouse study, specifying a 3\ W power envelope and pointing to XRBench [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench] still leaves the architect to fix the exact input traces, model versions, data distributions, and quality targets before two hardware proposals can be compared.

Recording those workload and compiler choices tells reviewers what was measured and which upstream software shifts would require repeating the experiment. Fixing the workload and software path, however, is not enough on its own, because evaluating a core or accelerator in isolation can still mislead whenever its traffic perturbs shared interconnects, memory pools, or rack power delivery. The architect also has to decide how far outward the system boundary must extend.

## How the Design Boundary Stretches from Sensors to Datacenters

```{=latex}
\suppressfloats[t]
```

The boundary of an architectural study determines which physical and queueing interactions the comparison can observe. If a candidate accelerator finishes a kernel faster in isolation but sends more intermediate data across a shared fabric, a device-level benchmark will rank it ahead even when network congestion slows the end-to-end service request. Whenever off-block traffic can flip which design wins, the evaluation boundary has to widen to include the shared resource. As the study boundary moves outward from an individual execution core at the bottom of the stack to warehouse-scale services at the top, each compute scale adds new comparison obligations (@fig-architecture-levers).

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The tall print-size scale diagram needs a full-page float option near its discussion. -->
![**The study boundary must include interactions that can change the decision.** Stacked from warehouse-scale deployment at the top down to core execution at the bottom, five compute scales illustrate how comparison obligations funnel outward as the system boundary expands upward from a core. A broader study may reuse component models; it need not reproduce every lower-level detail at the same fidelity.](images/fig-architecture-levers){#fig-architecture-levers width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Diagram of five architecture scales stacked from warehouse-scale system at the top down through wafer-scale system, system-on-chip or chiplet, accelerator, and core at the bottom, funneling outward as the system boundary expands upward from core to warehouse-scale. Each scale adds named obligations to a common comparison path feeding one cross-scale architecture comparison."}

At the top of that stack, warehouse-scale demand and availability requirements turn resource placement and sharing into architectural decisions across servers, networks, distributed runtimes, cooling loops, and facility power limits [@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer]. Within and across nodes, cache-coherent interconnects such as Compute Express Link (CXL) add further options for pooling and sharing memory across devices.[^fn-cxl-c02] These system-level mechanisms belong inside the study boundary whenever they can alter the target metric, whether tail request latency, sustained throughput, or total cost of ownership.

[^fn-cxl-c02]: **Compute Express Link (CXL)**: A cache-coherent interconnect standard for processors, accelerators, and memory devices. Its memory semantics and switching support allow architects to treat device-attached or pooled memory as a system-level provisioning decision [@CXLConsortium2026CXL].

Simulating all of those warehouse- and node-level interactions at cycle level is infeasible, so architects combine characterized component models with trace-driven or discrete-event simulators, hardware testbeds, and production telemetry. The composite model does not need uniform cycle accuracy everywhere, but it must preserve every interaction that can flip the ranking of candidates. Because independent trace replays miss network contention and mean response times hide the stragglers that govern tail latency at scale [@DeanBarroso2013TailAtScale], widening the system boundary requires coupling models across fidelity levels rather than running one brute-force simulator.

The practical rule is to choose the smallest system boundary that still captures every interaction capable of reversing the architectural decision. An isolated module boundary suffices for local pipeline timing, whereas an end-to-end service-latency study must include shared fabrics and pooled memory. Once that boundary is fixed, however, the hardware parameters, mapping choices, and compiler schedules inside it still multiply into far more candidates than detailed tools can run, raising the next practical question: how much of the resulting design space can a team actually afford to evaluate?

## Why Coupled Design Spaces Outgrow Manual Search {#sec-evaluation-capacity-bounds-search}

Within a chosen system boundary, hardware parameters, dataflow mappings, and compiler schedules combine to define the space of candidate designs. The raw number of combinations says little on its own about how hard that space is to search, because a billion candidates that an analytical model can score in milliseconds pose a very different engineering problem from a hundred candidates that each require days of RTL simulation and place-and-route.

Rather than evaluating every candidate at full fidelity, a practical exploration flow rules out illegal configurations first, screens the valid survivors with fast analytical models, and reserves slow cycle-level simulation and physical implementation for a handful of finalists. Whether a study is bottlenecked by generating valid candidates, screening them quickly, or verifying the finalists depends on which layer of the stack is being searched.

The four published tasks in @tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors illustrate how those bottlenecks shift across mapping, accelerator design-space exploration (DSE), block floorplanning, and tensor-compiler tuning.

Timeloop [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop], an analytical framework for mapping and evaluating deep neural network (DNN) accelerators, gives a concrete lower bound on how fast these spaces grow. For a convolutional neural network layer with seven nested loops (batch size, input channels, output channels, output height, output width, kernel height, and kernel width) and a four-level memory hierarchy, loop ordering and level-bypass choices alone produce $(7!)^4 \times (2^4)^3$ arrangements. The first factor counts the permutations of the seven loops at each of the four memory levels, while the second counts the binary bypass choices at those four levels for each of the three tensors (inputs, weights, and outputs). Loop-bound factorization enlarges this mapspace even further, so the expression is neither the full mapspace size nor a count of useful mappings; instead, it isolates two combinatorial factors before legality, buffer-capacity, and performance constraints prune away most candidates.

| **Architecture task** | **Scale anchor** | **Why candidate count is not enough** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| DNN accelerator mapping | Timeloop enumerates loop permutations, factorization choices, and level-bypass alternatives [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. | Mapping is itself a combinatorial problem; architecture evaluation depends on the mapper and its constraints. |
| DNN accelerator DSE | MAESTRO, an analytical cost model for estimating DNN dataflow performance, reports 480M candidates, 2.5M valid designs, and 0.17M designs/s [@KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO]. | Pruning rules determine which candidates are evaluated and which are never seen. |
| Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) block floorplanning | AlphaChip uses reinforcement learning to generate macro placements [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. | Reported gains depend on the cases, baselines, compute budgets, and downstream checks, which remain disputed in the reproduction, the reply, and the updated assessment [@ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement; @GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. |
| Tensor-program tuning | AutoTVM, a machine learning-based tensor program optimizer, describes tensor-operator search spaces on the order of billions of possible implementations for a single GPU operator [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. | Compiler schedules create a hardware-dependent search problem of their own. |
: **Large search spaces place different demands on evaluation.** Mapping, accelerator DSE, floorplanning, and tensor-program tuning combine candidate scale, validity constraints, feedback cost, and different evidence requirements. {#tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

\FloatBarrier

The remaining rows in @tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors show that combinatorial growth arises at every layer of the stack, but for different reasons. Timeloop and MAESTRO capture how quickly mapping and accelerator datapath parameters multiply, whereas AutoTVM shows that billions of valid compiler schedules remain even after the hardware is completely fixed. Macro floorplanning illustrates the opposite regime, where generating a candidate placement with reinforcement learning is fast, but establishing whether that placement actually routes and closes timing requires expensive physical-design tools. Even in MAESTRO, where an analytical model scoring 0.17M designs per second could sweep all 480M candidates in under an hour, fast screening is only the first step; the hard engineering decision is choosing which top-ranked candidates deserve slow RTL simulation and synthesis.

Plotted on a common logarithmic axis, the three count-based anchors from @tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors span roughly ten orders of magnitude (@fig-search-vs-eval-gap). Because they represent different kinds of quantities (a reported accelerator sweep, an order-of-magnitude compiler-schedule estimate, and a partial mapping lower bound), their spread illustrates how combinatorial scale varies across design layers rather than ranking the difficulty of the three problems.

```{python}
#| label: fig-search-vs-eval-gap
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Published architecture search spaces span roughly ten orders of magnitude.** Three scale anchors share
#|   a logarithmic axis: MAESTRO accelerator DSE ($4.8 \times 10^8$ candidates) [@KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO], AutoTVM tensor-program tuning
#|   ($\sim 10^9$ implementations) [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM], and a Timeloop mapspace lower bound from loop-ordering
#|   and bypass permutations ($2.6 \times 10^{18}$ configurations) [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. Filled markers indicate
#|   stated or computed counts; the hollow marker is an order-of-magnitude estimate. Candidate enumeration volume

Filled markers show a reported or computed count; the hollow AutoTVM marker shows an order-of-magnitude estimate."

timeloop_mapspace = factorial(7) ** 4 * (2**4) ** 3
```
