```{python}
row_axis(ax, len(rows))
top_log_axis(
    ax,
    xlim=(1e8, 4e19),
    xticks=[1e9, 1e12, 1e15, 1e18],
    xticklabels=["$10^{9}$", "$10^{12}$", "$10^{15}$", "$10^{18}$"],
    xlabel="search-space size (candidate configurations)",
)

for y, row in enumerate(rows):
    ax.axhline(y, color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.65, zorder=0)
    if row["stated"]:
        ax.scatter([row["value"]], [y], s=26, marker="o", facecolor=COLORS["designspace"], edgecolor=COLORS["designspace"], linewidth=1.0, zorder=3)
    else:
        ax.scatter([row["value"]], [y], s=26, marker="o", facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["designspace"], linewidth=1.2, zorder=3)
    ax.text(-0.86, y - 0.17, row["label"], transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.6, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["ink"], clip_on=False)
    ax.text(-0.86, y + 0.23, row["note"], transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=5.4, color=COLORS["muted"], clip_on=False)
    ax.text(1.04, y, row["right"], transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.1, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["designspace_ink"], clip_on=False)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

Across all of these layers, enumerating or proposing candidates is rarely what limits architectural progress. The real bottleneck is the cost of checking whether a candidate is physically buildable, how fast it runs on realistic workloads, and whether it is functionally correct.

## Why Physical Layout, Simulation, and Verification Slow the Loop

Blaming slow evaluation in general often sends an engineering team after the wrong bottleneck, because a group can spend weeks accelerating cycle-level simulation or training a fast performance predictor, only to watch its top-ranked candidates fail post-layout timing closure or stall in formal verification. Because no project can run every check on every candidate, an architect has to separate three distinct sources of evaluation cost before deciding which additional work will actually sharpen a comparison:

1. **Physical implementation:** Timing closure, wire routing, power delivery, and heat removal can change whether a candidate is feasible or competitive.
2. **Simulation throughput:** Detailed timing simulators, hardware emulators, and field-programmable gate array (FPGA) platforms trade setup effort against execution speed.
3. **Functional verification:** Tests and formal proofs must cover relevant behaviors and corner cases, including interactions absent from performance workloads.

Any of the three can limit a study, but physical constraints come first because they explain why a promising high-level estimate can fall apart once wires, power rails, and package limits enter the picture.

### Physical Constraints {#sec-physical-constraints-move-into-architecture}

That tension between fast early screening and physical detail shows up as soon as an architect compares candidate designs. A high-level model simple enough to screen many options may omit a local hotspot, a supply-voltage droop, or a routing bottleneck that reverses the outcome, whereas the detailed checks that expose those effects demand fuller design inputs and hours of tool runtime. The architect therefore has to decide which physical constraints must be represented early and which uncertainties can wait until a candidate is developed further.

Power delivery and heat removal illustrate how two physical constraints act on different timescales. When many execution units switch on together, the sudden current change can cause a transient supply droop across the resistance and inductance of the delivery network,[^fn-di-dt-drop-c02] and whether that droop causes a timing failure depends on the operating point and available voltage margin. Sustained activity raises a slower question: can the package remove heat from the locations where it is generated? In a stacked design, the placement of active logic and the heat-removal path matter alongside total power, so a single average-power estimate answers neither question.

[^fn-di-dt-drop-c02]: **Inductive voltage transients ($L \frac{di}{dt}$)**: Power delivery networks contain parasitic inductance ($L$) distributed across printed circuit board planes, package balls, and micro-bumps. When an ungated vector or matrix unit abruptly transitions from idle to full execution within one or two clock cycles, the rate of current change ($\frac{di}{dt}$) becomes large. The resulting induced voltage drop ($\Delta V = L \frac{di}{dt}$) compounds the steady-state resistive drop ($IR$), causing a transient voltage sag that can collapse the core supply rail below minimum operating voltage ($V_{\text{min}}$) and induce timing errors unless damped by on-die decoupling capacitors and conservative voltage guardbands.

Moving to a newer process node does not automatically resolve these physical interactions (@sec-fracturing-technology-dividend). Because standard logic cells, SRAM macros, and metal interconnects have different scaling behavior and layout rules, an architect revisiting our opening cache study cannot rely on a nominal process label; the comparison must estimate the area, access time, dynamic energy, and leakage of the available SRAM macro together with the wires that connect it.

The energy cost of moving data across those wires and memory arrays shows why physical locality dominates arithmetic count. Across the access widths and memory sizes compiled by @Horowitz2014Energy and labeled in @fig-data-movement-energy-scale, fetching operands from on-chip SRAM costs roughly two to three orders of magnitude more energy than a 32-bit integer addition, while going off chip to DRAM costs more than four orders of magnitude more. Because these 45\ nm reference values illustrate how easily a small reduction in arithmetic can be outweighed by extra memory traffic rather than supplying energy estimates for a current process, a system estimate must combine workload operation counts with energy costs characterized for its own implementation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-data-movement-energy-scale
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Data movement can dominate arithmetic energy.** Reference $45\ \text{nm}$ energy values from @Horowitz2014Energy
#|   demonstrate a disparity of more than four orders of magnitude between local arithmetic (0.1\ pJ for a 32-bit integer add)
#|   and memory access (10–100\ pJ for on-chip static random-access memory (SRAM), 1.3–2.6\ nJ for off-chip DRAM, a $13{,}000\text{--}26{,}000\times$
#|   energy penalty). Architectural comparisons must represent data locality, buffer hierarchies, and memory
#|   traffic rather than counting arithmetic operations in isolation. Transcribed order-of-magnitude anchors,
#|   not current-node device estimates.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale plot comparing arithmetic and memory-access energy, showing a 32-bit integer add at 0.1 picojoules, static random-access memory (SRAM) accesses from 10 to 100 picojoules, and an off-chip DRAM access range from 1.3 to 2.6 nanojoules."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style, draw_range_rows, row_axis, top_log_axis

# Source dataset: data/datasets/chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv (Horowitz, ISSCC 2014, 45 nm).
# Values are read from the CSV; ratios to the 32-bit integer add are computed here.
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    src = [r for r in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#"))]

baseline = float(src[0]["energy_low_pj"])


def _fmt_ratio(value):
    ratio = value / baseline
    return f"{ratio / 1000:.0f}k" if ratio >= 1000 and value >= 1000 else f"{ratio:.0f}"


rows = []
for r in src:
    low, high = float(r["energy_low_pj"]), float(r["energy_high_pj"])
    op, width = r["operation_or_access"], r["width_or_capacity"]
    if "SRAM" in op:
        capacity = width.replace(" 64 bit", "")
        label, note = f"{capacity} SRAM access", "64b access"
        color = COLORS["orange"] if high >= 100 else COLORS["green"]
    elif "DRAM" in op:
        label, note, color = "off-chip DRAM access", "64b access", COLORS["red"]
    else:
        label, note, color = f"{width.replace(' bit', 'b')} {op}", "local arithmetic", COLORS["blue"]
    right = f"{_fmt_ratio(low)}$\\times$" if low == high else f"{_fmt_ratio(low)}–{_fmt_ratio(high)}$\\times$"
    rows.append({"display_label": label, "display_note": note, "energy_low_pj": low,
                 "energy_high_pj": high, "right_label": right, "color": color})

apply_style()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.9, 3.2))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.40, right=0.80, top=0.82, bottom=0.08)

row_axis(ax, len(rows))
top_log_axis(
    ax,
    xlim=(0.06, 4000),
    xticks=[0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000],
    xticklabels=["0.1 pJ", "1 pJ", "10 pJ", "100 pJ", "1 nJ"],
    xlabel="rough energy per operation or access",
)
draw_range_rows(ax, rows, low_key="energy_low_pj", high_key="energy_high_pj", label_x=-0.82, right_x=1.04, label_fontsize=6.6, note_fontsize=5.4, right_fontsize=6.1, label_dy=-0.17, note_dy=0.23)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

To keep those implementation costs visible when comparing designs, we can group system energy by where the work occurs. The decomposition below separates computation, memory, interconnect, control, and leakage; each term must be estimated for the workload and implementation under study rather than read from historical reference ratios.
$$
E_{\mathrm{system}} = E_{\mathrm{compute}} + E_{\mathrm{memory}} + E_{\mathrm{interconnect}} + E_{\mathrm{control}} + E_{\mathrm{leakage}}
$${#eq-system-energy-decomposition}

Writing out @eq-system-energy-decomposition gives the memory hierarchy an explicit weight in the comparison. Just as the *memory wall* described by @WulfMcKee1995HittingMemoryWall depends on how often a program reaches slower memory levels and how much of that latency the processor can hide, $E_{\mathrm{memory}}$ depends on actual traffic across the hierarchy rather than on per-access energy alone.

Moving data among cores and accelerator tiles brings in $E_{\mathrm{interconnect}}$ alongside two distinct forms of congestion. At run time, offered traffic can exceed a network-on-chip link's capacity, causing queueing and backpressure even while arithmetic units have spare capacity; at layout time, the physical floorplan must also provide the metal tracks needed to route the chosen topology. Runtime network congestion and physical routing congestion interact through the floorplan, but they are separate phenomena tested by different tools.

Because these terms are coupled, optimizing one component in isolation can push cost into the others (@fig-waterbed-effect). A candidate that reduces $E_{\mathrm{compute}}$ while adding memory accesses and tile-to-tile communication will raise $E_{\mathrm{system}}$ whenever those added costs exceed the compute saving, causing a compute-only metric to rank the candidates incorrectly. Establishing whether that reversal occurs requires measuring both the workload's traffic and the implementation costs of each candidate.

![**A compute saving must be compared with the other energy changes it causes.** This dependency diagram identifies the terms needed to compare a candidate with its baseline. The sign of the total energy change depends on the sum of the changes in computation, memory, interconnect, control, and leakage; a lower compute term alone does not determine it. Boxes and arrows encode dependencies, not measured magnitudes.](images/fig-waterbed-effect){#fig-waterbed-effect width="100%" fig-alt="Unscaled dependency diagram connecting a compute-energy reduction and changes in memory, interconnect, control, and leakage to the total system energy change."}

Early analytical models can incorporate rough wire estimates to screen against such reversals, yet placement and routing settle the realized physical wire lengths, routing congestion, and parasitic capacitance [@KahngEtAl2011VLSIPhysicalDesign]. An automated search guided by an incomplete proxy score that omits data movement and wire parasitics can therefore promote configurations that look attractive in high-level screening (@fig-waterbed-effect) but fail physical implementation; spot-checking selected candidates with a post-layout model helps reveal how often that bias occurs for a given proxy and design.

The same multi-stage discipline applies to power delivery and heat. Early activity and placement estimates, including learned predictors such as PowerNet's IR-drop model [@XieEtAl2020PowerNet] within the inputs and conditions they cover, can flag a dense mapping that deserves closer inspection even when average power is acceptable. Because electrical supply droops and steady-state heat removal act on different timescales, however, thermal analysis and power-delivery analysis must address their respective effects separately, and passing a thermal check cannot establish that a rapid current transient is harmless.

Hardware power-management policies turn those electrical and thermal limits directly into performance effects. Adding 512-bit vector units to general-purpose CPU cores raises peak floating-point throughput, yet sustained AVX-512 execution on Intel's Skylake-generation server processors could trigger frequency-license offsets that lowered the clock for scalar work on the same core. Because the size of such effects varies by processor generation and peak vector width alone does not determine final application speed, architects must measure active-frequency policies alongside the exact mix of vector and nonvector work on the target processor.

Even after nominal clock targets are set, timing signoff must check that every path meets cycle limits across multiple analysis views that pair operating modes with specific process corners in static timing signoff tools such as Cadence Tempus [@Cadence2021Tempus].[^fn-pvt-corners-c02] A design can clear one view while failing another, and because physical-design tools rely on heuristic optimization, a single failed closure attempt rarely indicates whether the candidate microarchitecture or a flawed tool setup caused the failure. Comparing constraints, placement seeds, and repeated runs separates true design flaws from tool artifacts.[^fn-eda-tool-noise-c02]

[^fn-pvt-corners-c02]: **Multi-mode multi-corner (MMMC) timing closure**: Physical signoff tools evaluate a circuit across specified operating modes and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions. Slow analysis views expose setup-time violations, while fast views expose hold-time violations where data arrives too early relative to the receiving clock. The relevant temperature and voltage combinations come from characterized libraries; their ordering cannot be inferred from temperature alone. Advanced processes also require appropriate treatment of device self-heating and statistical on-chip variation, while processes with backside power delivery add its electrical and thermal effects. A candidate that meets cycle limits at nominal conditions may still fail timing or reliability checks in another required view.

[^fn-eda-tool-noise-c02]: **EDA tool non-determinism and noise floors**: Physical synthesis, placement, and detailed routing rely on stochastic heuristics, including simulated annealing, force-directed relaxation, and multi-threaded maze routing. Minor variations in netlist declaration order or random seed initialization can shift worst negative slack (WNS) and total wirelength on identical RTL. The size of that spread depends on the tool, design, and flow, so it must be measured for the flow in use; @sec-incremental-churn-dispersion reports one such measurement across twenty placement seeds. In automated AI exploration loops, agents can easily mistake an artifact of tool noise for an architectural breakthrough, or discard a superior microarchitecture because the placer hit an unfavorable local minimum. Bounded multi-seed calibration is necessary to separate true architectural merit from tool noise.

Detailed routing adds foundry design-rule checks to that signoff burden. Routing must satisfy restricted design rules, including minimum wire and via spacing [@KahngEtAl2011VLSIPhysicalDesign], so moving a single macro can spawn numerous violations, and repairing one route can disturb neighboring nets and expose fresh errors. When an automated flow cannot interpret or repair these markers, it shifts a repetitive cleanup and rerouting burden onto implementation engineers.

Consider how a Layer 2 floorplan optimizer can run into this friction. Suppose the optimizer sweeps macro coordinates $\theta$ inside a fixed die outline and scores each candidate with a fast wirelength estimate or learned surrogate. Such proxies track average wirelength well while missing local pin density, routing-channel blockages, and multi-corner timing slack. If the favored placements crowd memory interfaces into dense clusters, the router may run short of tracks and return timing violations and design-rule markers that the proxy never predicted. Confined to its declared parameter container, the optimizer cannot reshape pipeline registers, re-partition blocks, or change interface contracts, so the repair falls to implementation engineers unless the proxy is recalibrated or the search is allowed to move those boundaries. How often this happens depends on the design, the proxy, and the flow; the scenario identifies a failure mode to check for, not a measured rate.

Diagnosing why such a physical run failed requires the exact design files and assumptions that produced it. Retaining the RTL, parameters, constraints, and implementation outputs lets an architect distinguish a genuine microarchitectural problem from a mismatched input file. Because EDA tools also consume physical and timing representations beyond RTL, including Library Exchange Format / Design Exchange Format (LEF/DEF) and Liberty timing files,[^fn-lef-def-c02] preparing and preserving compatible inputs is part of architectural evaluation itself (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces).

[^fn-lef-def-c02]: **LEF/DEF and Liberty**: In place-and-route flows, LEF carries the abstract physical information used to place and connect blocks, while DEF records design-specific physical information, such as placement and routing, even before those steps are complete [@Si2LEFDEF]. Meanwhile, Liberty provides characterized cell models covering timing, power, noise, and related behaviors [@Synopsys2012LibertyFormat]. Physical design relies on these implementation formats to expose details omitted from high-level architectural descriptions.

Multi-fidelity methods manage these tool costs by pairing inexpensive screening models with selected evaluations that resolve their important omissions [@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. Gate-level functional simulation, static timing analysis, and thermal analysis each answer a different question, so running a more expensive tool helps only when it addresses the specific uncertainty that could change the architectural decision.

While an inexpensive energy proxy supports early screening, finalists need an accurate power and contention model before the team commits to a design. A microarchitecture can lead on advertised peak throughput yet fall behind on real application workloads once shared-resource stalls and power limits take hold, as one generation of AMD processors illustrated in practice.

::: {.callout-war-story title="A design that won on the spec sheet"}
**The claim.** In the Bulldozer generation (Zambezi, 2011), AMD grouped two integer cores behind a shared front end and floating-point unit while pushing clock frequency hard [@BurgessEtAl2011Bulldozer]. Core counts and frequencies are easy to advertise, so they made compelling marketing points. In sharing those structures, the design team traded per-thread capacity for aggregate throughput.
**The gap.** Those figures did not reflect how real workloads used the machine. The shared structures became bottlenecks when threads competed for them, and the higher frequencies raised power draw. The later FX-9590 part carried a 220\ W TDP [@AMDFXQuickReference].
**The lesson.** Because core count and clock rate alone cannot settle the comparison, shared structures must be evaluated with workloads that expose contention alongside power and frequency behavior, which explains why AMD's later Zen design placed renewed emphasis on per-core performance and efficiency [@AMDZen].
:::

### Simulation Throughput and Fidelity {#sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive}

Running realistic workloads detailed enough to expose such contention quickly turns simulation speed into the next constraint. Once a performance model captures cycle-level resource conflicts, longer traces and larger candidate pools compete directly for compute clusters, tool licenses, and engineering review time. The practical question is how much representative program behavior the available evaluation budget can cover.

Detailed software simulators run orders of magnitude slower than native execution. The 2013 zsim study, for example, reported detailed gem5, Flexus, and MARSS configurations running at about two hundred thousand target instructions per host second [@ZSim]. While present throughput depends on the simulator, configuration, workload, and host machine, that historical rate shows why a team must measure its own simulator speed before multiplying workload lengths and candidate counts into an evaluation budget.

When software simulation is too slow or too abstract, teams choose among architectural simulators, compiled RTL simulation, hardware emulators, and FPGA platforms that trade setup effort against execution capacity while modeling different physical and behavioral details. Whereas a fast architectural simulator simplifies cycle-level timing interactions, Verilator executes an RTL model directly, and FireSim uses FPGA acceleration to run full-system, cycle-exact RTL simulations [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Even a cycle-exact RTL model omits routed wire delays and package thermals, however, so each tool's fidelity must be judged for the specific behavior it represents, and the useful choice is the one whose model and execution speed answer the study's question at an acceptable total cost.

If running full workloads remains too slow, sampling can cut execution cost without stripping out microarchitectural detail. SimPoint selects representative program regions [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint], while SMARTS uses statistical sampling with explicit error bounds [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. Analytical screening, sampled detailed simulation, and full-workload execution can then work in stages, provided the study records which program behavior the sample represents, how cache and predictor warmup are handled, and which conclusions still require full runs.

Staged simulation always carries two allocation risks: a coarse early filter can discard a promising candidate prematurely or pass an unsuitable one into expensive cycle-accurate evaluation. Even more important, reducing uncertainty about performance on benchmark traces never proves that the hardware works across every legal state transition the design permits. Establishing correctness across those unexercised states is the job of verification.

### Verification Bottlenecks

Verification is demanding because hardware state grows exponentially with sequential storage. Adding a single flip-flop doubles the number of encoded states, so a design with $n$ state elements can encode up to $2^n$ configurations. Although reset sequences and valid transition logic restrict the reachable subset to a fraction of that space, the reachable state graph in any realistic processor or accelerator is still far too large to check by brute-force enumeration.

Rather than enumerating every state, verification teams combine functional coverage targets, SystemVerilog Assertions, formal checks, constrained-random and directed tests, regression suites, and unresolved-defect reviews. Functional coverage tracks which planned behaviors and requirements the tests have exercised, but completing a coverage target only shows that the listed scenarios ran, not that every possible bug is absent. Whenever an exploration loop changes a block's architectural organization, the candidate can require new assertions and test plans even when much of the surrounding implementation is reused.

Verification effort therefore belongs beside power, performance, and area (PPA) when architects compare candidates. A speculative cache-coherence protocol might show an impressive throughput gain in cycle-level simulation and still be the wrong choice if verifying its transient states and race conditions exceeds the design-program budget.

Checking such protocols draws on both dynamic simulation and formal methods, which provide different kinds of assurance. Whereas simulation exercises selected behaviors under supplied stimuli, a completed formal proof establishes a stated property for all behaviors covered by the model and its assumptions, provided the solver can complete the proof. When a full proof is intractable, bounded model checking searches behaviors up to a specified cycle depth without proving correctness beyond that bound, while combinational equivalence checking asks whether two combinational descriptions compute the same Boolean function. These techniques complement one another so long as their scopes and assumptions remain explicit [@Clarke2018ModelChecking].

Even with both dynamic and formal tools in hand, the semiconductor industry has grappled with verification scaling for over a quarter of a century. As far back as 2001, the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS) Design chapter declared verification "a bottleneck that has now reached crisis proportions" [@ITRS2001Design], and the SRC's MAPT roadmap warns of a widening verification gap across future technology transitions [@SemiconductorResearchCorporation2023MAPT]. This history is reason enough to check verification capacity whenever someone proposes generating architectural candidates faster, even though verification will not be the limiting constraint in every design program.

Industry staffing surveys offer a quantitative view of how the verification share introduced in @sec-moonshot grew over time. In the 2022 Wilson Research Group study, demand for verification engineers on integrated circuit (IC) and ASIC projects grew at about 6.2% per year from 2007 to 2022, against about 2.7% per year for design engineers [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. Compounded over fifteen years, project verification staffing reached roughly two and a half times its 2007 level while design staffing reached about one and a half times (@fig-verification-demand-scissors). Those curves track relative project staffing rather than the marginal time needed to verify one additional candidate, but they show where engineering effort has concentrated.

```{python}
#| label: fig-verification-demand-scissors
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Verification staffing grew faster than design staffing.** Mean peak staffing per IC/ASIC project
#|   indexed to a 2007 baseline demonstrates that verification engineer demand grew by 146% (a 6.2%
#|   compound annual growth rate [CAGR], reaching $\approx 2.46\times$) from 2007 to 2022, while design engineer demand grew by 50%
#|   (a 2.7% CAGR, reaching $\approx 1.50\times$) [@Foster2021WilsonPart8; @Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. Filled markers indicate
#|   printed data labels from published survey figures; hollow 2022 markers represent chart-read approximations
#|   constrained by the study's stated growth rates.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Two-line chart indexing engineer demand to 2007, with verification-engineer demand rising to about 2.5 times its 2007 level by 2022 while design-engineer demand reaches about 1.5 times, opening a widening gap between the lines."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Mean peak engineers per IC/ASIC project, Wilson Research Group / Siemens EDA
# functional-verification studies (Foster's published summaries).
# Source data: data/datasets/chapter2-wilson-verification-staffing.csv. Rows with
# evidence_type == chart_read_constrained are drawn hollow; growth labels are computed.
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-wilson-verification-staffing.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    staff = [r for r in csv.DictReader(fh) if r["year"].isdigit()]
years = [int(r["year"]) for r in staff]
design = [float(r["design_engineers_mean_peak"]) for r in staff]
verif = [float(r["verification_engineers_mean_peak"]) for r in staff]
printed = [r["evidence_type"] == "printed_data_label" for r in staff]

design_idx = [v / design[0] for v in design]
verif_idx = [v / verif[0] for v in verif]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.65, 2.3))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.80, top=0.93, bottom=0.19)

ax.plot(years, verif_idx, color=COLORS["green"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
ax.plot(years, design_idx, color=COLORS["blue"], linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
for x, v, d, solid in zip(years, verif_idx, design_idx, printed):
    if solid:
        ax.scatter([x], [v], s=22, color=COLORS["green"], zorder=3)
        ax.scatter([x], [d], s=20, marker="s", color=COLORS["blue"], zorder=3)
    else:
        ax.scatter([x], [v], s=26, facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["green"], linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)
        ax.scatter([x], [d], s=24, marker="s", facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["blue"], linewidths=1.1, zorder=3)

ax.text(years[-1] + 0.6, verif_idx[-1], f"verification\nengineers (+{(verif_idx[-1] - 1) * 100:.0f}%)",
        va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["green"], clip_on=False)
ax.text(years[-1] + 0.6, design_idx[-1], f"design\nengineers (+{(design_idx[-1] - 1) * 100:.0f}%)",
        va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["blue"], clip_on=False)

ax.set_xlim(years[0] - 1, years[-1] + 1)
ax.set_ylim(0.9, 2.7)
ax.set_xticks(years)
ax.set_yticks([1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5])
ax.set_yticklabels(["1.0$\\times$", "1.5$\\times$", "2.0$\\times$", "2.5$\\times$"])
ax.set_ylabel(f"mean peak demand vs. {years[0]}", fontsize=7)
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=6.5, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(axis="y", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

While the indexed curves in @fig-verification-demand-scissors do not isolate a single cause or determine the bottleneck in a particular project, they show why verification capacity deserves explicit attention in a design plan. A natural follow-up question is what those same industry surveys report about project time and first-silicon outcomes alongside that staffing growth.

Across the 2010 to 2020 Wilson Research Group studies, the published mean share of project time spent in verification stayed between 53% and 57%, even as first-silicon success fell from about 32% in 2020 to 24% in 2022 (@fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors). Although the 2024 study reported 14% first-silicon success [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy; @Foster2025WilsonVerification2024], survey recruitment changed that year from industry lists to a qualified sample provider, and this methodological break, together with elevated nonresponse on some 2024 questions, prevents treating the two periods as equivalent measurements of the same population [@Foster2026SurveyMethodologyEvolution]. Even within the consistent pre-2024 series, the reports show substantial verification work alongside persistent silicon respins, most often associated with logic or functional flaws rather than added verification causing worse outcomes.

![**Verification surveys report substantial effort and persistent first-silicon failures.** Published verification time (2010–2020), first-silicon success (2014–2024), and staffing ratios (2007–2024); hollow staffing points are derived from growth rates [@Foster2013WilsonPart5; @Foster2015TrendsFunctionalVerification; @Foster2021WilsonPart8; @Foster2021WilsonPart12; @Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy; @Foster2023WilsonPart12; @Foster2025WilsonVerification2024]. The 2024 recruitment change breaks direct comparability with 2007–2022 [@Foster2026SurveyMethodologyEvolution]. Lines connect available observations without establishing causality.](images/fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors){#fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors width="100%" fig-alt="Survey chart showing verification time shares of 53 to 57 percent through 2020 and first-silicon success of about 32 percent in 2020 and 24 percent in 2022. A shaded methodological break separates the 2024 result of 14 percent and its staffing ratio from the earlier series."}

The reported respin causes span logic bugs, analog integration, clock-domain crossings, timing paths, and hardware-firmware interactions [@Foster2025WilsonVerification2024]. Clock-domain crossings, for example, require attention to physical metastability as well as the logical sequence seen by a digital testbench.[^fn-metastability-c02] Running more random stimulus alone rarely exercises such rare boundary interactions; catching them takes directed tests, suitable constraints, assertions, and formal analysis tuned to the specific failure mechanism.

[^fn-metastability-c02]: **Metastability and clock-domain crossings (CDCs)**: A bistable storage element can enter a metastable state when an asynchronous input violates setup or hold timing constraints; its settling time has no guaranteed finite upper bound. Signals crossing asynchronous clock domains need a suitable crossing scheme, such as a multi-stage synchronizer for a single control signal or a handshake and asynchronous first-in, first-out queue for data transfers. These schemes reduce failure risk and preserve the intended communication, while ordinary cycle-accurate testbenches do not represent the intermediate analog voltages.

When a defect slips past those checks into fabricated silicon, its cost depends on how it can be repaired, because some escaped bugs permit a firmware or software workaround at the price of performance or features, whereas others require revised silicon. Intel's \$475M charge associated with the Pentium floating-point division defect illustrates the potential cost of a shipped arithmetic error [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Intel1995PentiumCharge], while Spectre and Meltdown illustrate a different failure mode in which speculative microarchitectural state undermines software's security assumptions [@LippEtAl2018Meltdown; @KocherEtAl2019Spectre]. Together these cases explain why signoff teams push for early detection without establishing a single universal cost multiplier for every late defect.

That signoff standard directly shapes how we evaluate machine-generated hardware candidates before their performance even matters. Even on small modules, published RTL-generation benchmarks report frequent failures at syntax parsing, interface compliance, and functional testing [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM; @WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. Passing those module-level tests still does not establish timing closure or system-level correctness, which is why a plausible RTL draft is only a starting point. How long it takes to produce and check a candidate depends on its scope, how much of the existing verification infrastructure can be reused, and the required assurance; there is no fixed generation-to-verification ratio across abstraction levels.

The survey data also bound what Layer 1 point assistance can deliver on its own. Although a generator that drafts an isolated leaf module or testbench inside a human-specified pipeline speeds up one step of implementation, project budgets are dominated by the surrounding integration and checking work. Verification staffing grew at more than twice the annual rate of design staffing (@fig-verification-demand-scissors), verification occupied more than half of reported project time in the 2010 to 2020 studies (@fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors), and the cost breakdown in @sec-design-cost-pressure assigns most of a leading-node budget to software, verification, and IP qualification. Faster drafting therefore yields a net gain only when the drafted modules do not add more integration and debugging work than they save, such as reconnecting mismatched ports, resolving clock-domain crossings, clearing lint violations, and diagnosing corner-case deadlocks. Whether Layer 1 assistance saves total engineering time is a measurement a team must make on its own workflow rather than a conclusion to assume in either direction.

Asking the same generator to write the tests does not escape this bottleneck by itself. When one model drafts both a design and its testbench from the same specification, a shared misreading of an edge case can appear in both artifacts, so that the tests pass while the hardware is wrong, reproducing the correlated-failure trap that @sec-moonshot introduced through the Knight–Leveson experiment [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion]. Trustworthy verification therefore needs a reference the generator cannot edit, such as assertions derived from the architectural contract or a golden reference model (@sec-feedback-verification-trust).

Whenever candidate architectures differ in the testbenches, formal properties, and integration work they require, that verification effort belongs in the architectural comparison alongside PPA. Reusing a familiar interface preserves much of that existing verification investment, whereas changing the microarchitectural organization demands new checks. Together with physical implementation and software bring-up, those engineering costs determine how many promising designs a program can afford to develop.

\FloatBarrier

## The Economics of Specialized Silicon {#sec-design-cost-pressure}

```{=latex}
\suppressfloats[t]
```

The implementation, software, and verification work described above comes out of a finite development budget. Much of that work is non-recurring engineering (NRE), the upfront investment in design, software, and qualification that precedes volume production. The scale of that upfront cost shapes both which architecture a program chooses and how many alternatives it can afford to develop in detail.

Public estimates show how steeply that investment rises toward the leading edge (@fig-design-cost-by-node). In the widely quoted series from International Business Strategies (IBS), a 2018 estimate put IC design cost at \$51.3M for a 28\ nm planar device, \$297.8M at 7\ nm, and \$542.2M at 5\ nm [@LaPedus2018BigTrouble3nm], while the Semiconductor Industry Association reports the same order of magnitude, placing a 5\ nm design above \$540M in 2020 [@SemiconductorIndustryAssociation2026ChipDesign]. Arm's 2023 prospectus, citing a July 2022 IBS series, estimates \$249M at 7\ nm and \$725M at 2\ nm [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. Because the two IBS vintages disagree at 7\ nm, each series rests on its own assumptions about die size, IP reuse, and what counts as design cost; although individual project budgets vary widely around any of these figures, both series show development cost climbing sharply at advanced nodes.

```{python}
#| label: fig-design-cost-by-node
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Leading-node design-cost estimates rise steeply, and they depend on the estimate's vintage.** Each bar is an
#|   International Business Strategies (IBS) estimate, labeled with the year of the IBS series it comes from
#|   [@LaPedus2018BigTrouble3nm; @ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. The two vintages differ at 7\ nm (\$298M versus \$249M),
#|   so the bars are published estimates under different assumptions, not a controlled node-scaling series or universal project prices.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of IC design-cost estimates by process node. The 2018 estimates are 51 million dollars at 28 nanometers, 298 million at 7 nanometers, and 542 million at 5 nanometers. The 2022 estimates, drawn hatched, are 249 million at 7 nanometers and 725 million at 2 nanometers."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Source data: data/datasets/chapter2-leading-node-design-cost.csv (rows with plotted == yes).
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-leading-node-design-cost.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    rows = [r for r in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")) if r["plotted"] == "yes"]
# Largest node first; within a node, older vintage first.
rows.sort(key=lambda r: (-float(r["node_nm"]), r["estimate_vintage"]))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.9))
positions = list(range(len(rows)))
for pos, r in zip(positions, rows):
    cost = float(r["cost_musd"])
    newer = r["estimate_vintage"].endswith("2022")
    ax.barh(pos, cost, height=0.58, color=COLORS["constraints_tint"], edgecolor=COLORS["constraints"],
            linewidth=1.4, hatch="////" if newer else None, zorder=3)
    ax.text(cost + 12, pos, f"${cost:,.0f}M", va="center", ha="left", fontsize=7,
            fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"], zorder=4)
    ax.text(cost + 100, pos, r["estimate_vintage"], va="center", ha="left", fontsize=6,
            color=COLORS["muted"], zorder=4)

ax.set_yticks(positions)
ax.set_yticklabels([f"{float(r['node_nm']):g} nm" for r in rows], fontsize=7, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlim(0, 1000)
ax.set_xlabel("Estimated IC design cost (US$M)", fontsize=7, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.5)
ax.grid(True, axis="x", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.45, zorder=0)
for spine in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

A breakdown of that design budget shows where automation has room to change total project cost. In the IBS 2\ nm estimate cited by Arm, software development, verification, and IP qualification together account for 71% of the total spend [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. Although that split reflects one estimate's cost model rather than the critical path of every chip program, it explains why faster RTL drafting alone cannot be assumed to eliminate most development expense.

That 71% to 29% split also frames a testable hypothesis about where each operational layer could reduce NRE, which only measurements from real programs can confirm. Because the prospectus does not separate RTL writing from the rest of the remaining 29%, that smaller slice cannot be read as the cost of drafting or physical design alone. Point assistance (Layer 1) that drafts leaf RTL acts on only part of that 29% remainder, so its net effect on NRE depends on whether the drafted code saves more implementation time than it adds in review, integration, and verification work. Parameter search inside a qualified container (Layer 2) keeps existing interface verification and qualified IP intact, which holds down new verification cost while limiting which architectural changes the search can reach. An AI-native design system (Layer 3) could reduce the 71% share only if it generated verification collateral, compiler support, and qualification evidence that reviewers could sign off at lower total cost than conventional practice; the public end-to-end demonstration examined in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect does not report that comparison.

How heavily that upfront NRE weighs on each chip depends on production volume. A simple accounting model makes the relationship explicit:

$$
C_{\mathrm{unit}} = C_{\mathrm{variable}} + \frac{C_{\mathrm{NRE}}}{V},
$$

where $C_{\mathrm{variable}}$ is the average manufacturing, packaging, and test cost per shipped unit, $C_{\mathrm{NRE}}$ is the allocated development investment, and $V$ is shipment volume. Within the variable term, die area $A$ and defect density $D_0$ govern silicon cost per good die (approximated in the Poisson model by $Y=e^{-A D_0}$, though defect clustering and other manufacturing effects require more detailed yield models). Because smaller dies reduce the silicon discarded when pre-assembly testing detects a defect, chiplet disaggregation can lower die cost, even as assembly yield, die-to-die interfaces, and advanced packaging take back part of that gain depending on the product's process and packaging parameters. Although this accounting model omits financing, pricing, and time-to-market effects, it exposes why a specialized design that saves enough energy or system cost to justify its development must carry a larger share of $C_{\mathrm{NRE}}$ per unit at lower volume, unless the team expands effective volume by reusing a modular chiplet across multiple products.

For a mobile-XR program, the architectural question is whether the efficiency and capability gains of custom silicon justify the hardware, software, and verification investment at the product's anticipated shipment volume. Reusing qualified IP, retaining programmable engines for changing workloads, or stepping back from the most expensive process node can improve that economic balance, while trading away some combination of power, performance, or schedule. A sound comparison weighs those coupled consequences together rather than assuming either that custom silicon is unaffordable or that specialization always pays for itself.

The compute and engineering budget spent evaluating candidates during the study follows the same logic. Spending more on a cycle-level simulation or integration test pays off when it resolves an uncertainty that would otherwise force an expensive redesign, just as generating more candidates pays off when those candidates open genuinely better design options. Both investments are worth their cost only to the extent that the complete study learns enough to improve the final decision for the resources it consumes, bringing the chapter's separate pressures together inside a single design loop.

## Compounding Loop Pressures {#sec-compounding-design-loop-pressure}

Although the preceding sections examined workload drift, physical effects, verification, and silicon economics one at a time, a design study encounters them together. A different memory organization may need new compiler support, which alters memory traffic and shifts both the physical floorplan and the system power comparison; some candidate designs can reuse existing testbenches, while others require fresh verification work. The effort required to learn from one alternative therefore depends on everything downstream of the proposal, not just on the cost of proposing it.

Because these stages are tightly coupled, speeding up one step in isolation often shifts the bottleneck elsewhere. If a team generates candidate designs faster without adding simulator licenses or verification capacity, the simulation queue simply grows longer. Design-space size and evaluation capacity are different quantities, and enlarging the first does nothing to expand the second.

Rather than hunting for a single universal bottleneck, engineering teams have to measure which stage is actually holding up the next decision. In practice, teams can track the age and length of simulation or verification queues, record the fraction of generated candidates rejected as illegal, count repeated tool runs caused by shifting inputs, and monitor where tool results sit waiting for expert judgment. Industry trends supply useful context, but only measurements from the program itself can show what is constraining it.

The MAESTRO anchor in @tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors shows why a team should inspect the work on both sides of a fast step before paying for a faster optimizer. Because MAESTRO's analytical model makes a large space of dataflow mappings cheap to score, the bottleneck in a study that uses it rarely sits inside the analytical evaluation itself. Upstream, the rankings depend on the workload description, since changed layer shapes or batch sizes can make an otherwise accurate analytical winner irrelevant to deployment. Downstream, turning a top-ranked mapping into hardware requires physical and verification checks that the analytical tier cannot supply, exposing two distinct bottlenecks on either side of the model.

Looking across the whole loop also separates slow tools from wasted runs. A simulator run against an outdated workload or misconfigured memory model occupies a compute slot without helping resolve the architecture question, even when the job finishes cleanly. When the team fixes those inputs before launching runs, useful throughput rises without making the simulator itself run any faster.

That gap between raw drafting speed and verified progress extends the classic *design productivity gap*, documented in the 1999 ITRS, restated in its 2001 edition [@ITRS2001Design], and reiterated in the SRC and Semiconductor Industry Association Decadal Plan [@SRCSIA2021DecadalPlan]. Earlier shifts in abstraction made larger chips tractable through logic synthesis and reusable IP blocks. When modern tools make it cheaper to construct candidate designs, the corresponding challenge is whether simulation, verification, and human review can absorb the additional work.

Not every constraint shows up as a tool queue, however. A study may stall because it is waiting for a missing workload trace or foundry constraint, or because every candidate permitted by the current hardware template misses the target. When the template itself cannot meet the target, evaluating the same family of designs faster will not produce a feasible chip; the architect has to reconsider the hardware organization, or the requirements, before scheduling more runs.

When the template is viable and proposals are flowing, a backlog grows whenever a program sends more candidates into evaluation and review than those stages complete over the same interval (@fig-scissors-gap). Proposal generation determines how many candidates are available, while screening and selection decide which ones enter the checking loop. Raw candidate counts can obscure a growing imbalance because one proposal may finish a fast check in seconds while another ties up simulation, physical checks, and human reviewers for days. Teams therefore need to compare arrivals and completions within each checking stage alongside the verification effort each candidate requires, either filtering candidates more strictly upfront or adding capacity at the limiting stage to rebalance the loop.

The three operational layers affect that backlog through both the volume of work they send downstream and the architectural boundaries they can change. Point assistance (Layer 1) lowers the cost of drafting modules or tests, which can swell the backlog if the team submits more drafts without expanding checking capacity. Parameter search inside a fixed container (Layer 2) automates selection using fast surrogates or direct physical checks while keeping interfaces stable, whereas an AI-native design system (Layer 3) can also change the interfaces and organization under study, creating new verification obligations. Because all three layers must preserve the evidence required to trust the final result, whether an intervention shrinks or grows the backlog depends on how candidates are filtered, how much checking capacity is available, and how often surviving proposals fail later review. That outcome has to be measured on the workflow rather than assumed from the layer alone.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The print-size workflow needs flexible placement beside the conditional backlog discussion. -->
![**Backlog depends on admitted work and completed checks.** This unscaled flow diagram separates proposal generation, admission, evaluation, and review. Waiting work grows at a stage when admissions exceed completions over the same interval; candidate counts must be interpreted alongside the different checking costs they impose. Admission and staged screening control how much generated work reaches the limited resources. The diagram specifies no measured rates or trend with architectural scope.](images/fig-scissors-gap){#fig-scissors-gap width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Unscaled flow diagram connecting proposal generation, admission, evaluation, and review to a completed decision. Waiting work is distinguished from completed checks; admission and screening determine which proposals enter the checking loop."}

Queue wait times, arrival rates, and completed checks turn @fig-scissors-gap into a practical diagnosis for a live program. When a generator makes drafting cheaper, a team can easily respond by sending more work into simulation and review, spending the saved drafting effort on extra downstream runs. A classic observation from resource economics explains why total demand need not fall when one activity becomes cheaper.

::: {.callout-law title="The Jevons Paradox of Automated Generation"}
**The principle.** Greater efficiency can encourage increased consumption that outstrips the initial savings, a rebound effect Jevons documented for coal consumption [@Jevons1865CoalQuestion]. In automated chip design, cheaper proposal generation can increase total resource consumption if the team responds by sending many more candidates into evaluation and review while downstream capacity stays fixed.

**The design implication.** When cheaper RTL generation leads a team to submit more candidates to simulation and physical implementation checks, demand for compute clusters and EDA licenses rises. The drafting saving remains real, yet the complete study can still consume more resources overall.

**The response.** Decide how many candidates are worth running through slow simulators and verification tools and which checks each candidate needs, then measure total effort alongside useful results. Selective filtering and staged screening provide practical controls (@sec-law-jevons-paradox in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

## Where AI Can Relieve the Bottlenecks {#sec-where-ai-assistance-targets-design-pressures}

A bottleneck diagnosis pays off only when it changes where the team spends its automation budget. If a study cannot start evaluating an idea because a working RTL block or testbench is missing, a generator that drafts that artifact moves the project forward. If hundreds of candidates already sit waiting for simulation, adding another generator only deepens the delay, whereas a fast screening model or automated tool triage can help clear the queue. The very same method can therefore accelerate one program and slow down another.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
```

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Relieve the true limiting constraint"}
**The principle.** Target optimization directly at the bottleneck that actively delays the design decision. Common limiting factors include stale architectural models, long physical simulation runtimes, unpruned candidate sets, and the time senior engineers spend triaging failures.

**The application.** Judge whether assistance reduces the total effort or calendar delay needed to answer the architecture question, counting preparation and review work alongside the step that became faster and preserving the checks the decision requires. Because relieving one bottleneck often exposes the next, the limiting work can shift as the study progresses.
:::

Different bottlenecks call for different forms of assistance, from pulling together scattered design information and screening candidates to drafting testbenches and guiding search (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization develops the underlying method choices). When changing software keeps shifting workload behavior, for instance, an automated regression pipeline can rerun the benchmark suite with a new compiler and flag any change in candidate rankings. Assistance can help explain which compiler transformation caused the shift or spot an input mismatch, though the comparison still has to distinguish a genuine hardware improvement from a changed task. Much of this work is served well by conventional automation, without a learned model.

The rows in @tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound pair each kind of limiting work with how AI might help, the engineering effort it could reduce, and the checks that still establish the result. Keeping the potential savings beside the required evidence stops a team from mistaking a faster local task for a completed architectural comparison.

| **Limiting work** | **How AI might help** | **Engineering work it could reduce** | **What still establishes the result** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Context is scattered or stale | Reconcile workload, interface, tool, and result information; flag missing details or stale assumptions. | Manual search across reports, repositories, traces, and prior studies. | Source provenance, versioning, coverage, and architectural judgment that the information is sufficient. |
| Strong evaluation is scarce | Estimate performance, power, physical risk, or uncertainty before a stronger tool is run. | High-fidelity evaluations spent on candidates unlikely to change design decisions. | Calibration against stronger tools, coverage of the relevant design region, and checks on finalists. |
| A needed artifact is missing | Draft RTL, compiler code, tests, constraints, or candidate organizations. | Repetitive artifact creation and the initial pass through a design choice. | Interface rules, compilation or synthesis, verification, and physical checks appropriate to the artifact. |
| The choice space exceeds the budget | Search mappings, schedules, parameters, or topologies under stated objectives and constraints. | Manual sweeps and repeated selection among large numbers of choices. | A complete objective, legal choices, matched evaluation budgets, and stronger evaluation of the selected result. |
| Tool operation or triage consumes attention | Configure tools, launch runs, classify failures, compare reports, and route uncertain cases. | Repeated tool operation and initial result triage. | Clean tool state, reproducible commands, declared tool results, and expert review where required. |
: **Match assistance to the limiting work and retain the necessary checks.** Each row identifies a possible saving and the evidence needed to use its output in a design decision. {#tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound tbl-colwidths="[22,28,24,26]"}

How those forms of assistance fit into a project depends on which operational layer organizes the workflow and how much of the design the automated work is allowed to change. Among the bottlenecks in @tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound, point assistance (Layer 1) fits cases where one artifact is missing and the surrounding design is settled; its output still passes through the integration and verification work described earlier. Automated search inside a fixed container (Layer 2) fits cases where the choice space exceeds the evaluation budget but the interfaces are already sound. That layer reaches its limit when no permitted parameter change can relieve the bottleneck, such as when neither local reuse nor batching can compensate for a fixed offload path. An AI-native design system (Layer 3) becomes a candidate response when the current hardware template itself rules out better organizations, though its broader exploration still requires checks matched to the claim, including static timing analysis, design rules, formal properties, and power integrity where relevant. Prediction, generation, and optimization can contribute across all three layers; what separates them is how the design work is organized and which architectural choices it can revisit.

Any honest comparison also has to count the cost of building and running the assistance itself. A learned surrogate may require training data from expensive simulations or synthesis runs; generated candidates require verification; and tool-using systems consume compute, licenses, and engineer review time. Those investments can be worthwhile, but leaving them out of the accounting makes displaced work look like a net saving.

Once those setup and checking costs are counted, a team should set AI assistance aside whenever an established deterministic method already solves the limiting task within budget. A learned method has a weak case when representative training data are unavailable, when an adequate independent check cannot be constructed, or when training, inference, tool calls, and added review cost more than the manual engineering work they save. Where analytical evaluation is already cheap, replacing it with a learned surrogate saves little, whereas a screening predictor calibrated against expensive cycle simulation or physical checks can be worth its setup cost regardless of the raw candidate count. When the primary obstacle is an infeasible requirement, the right response is to reformulate the architecture question or stop the search rather than automate it.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
```

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="No single method carries the Lighthouse moonshot"}
**Context.** The Lighthouse study begins with an XRBench-class mobile workload, a 64-bit RISC-V basis, a 3\ W target, and a 3\ nm-class process, leaving workload instances, memory organization, compiler support, and implementation choices to be developed during the study. The earlier cache and offload examples show why those choices have to be evaluated together across the operational layers.

**Application.** A Layer 1 approach might ask a generator to draft an isolated vector arithmetic leaf cell or scratchpad controller, leaving engineers to connect buses, resolve clock-domain crossings, and debug races. A Layer 2 approach might fix the 64-bit pipeline and sweep cache capacities and loop-unroll factors against a cycle simulator. That search reaches its limit if no permitted configuration can keep memory traffic within the 3\ W budget or relieve routing congestion; expanding the search then requires revisiting the container's boundaries.

A Layer 3 AI-native design system, if one could be built for this problem, would be permitted to set the fixed processor template aside and propose a streaming tensor datapath, custom arithmetic, tiled scratchpad memories, and matched compiler loop schedules from the XRBench intent and formal signoff assertions. To check whether those candidates meet the 3\ W target, the study must run workload-dependent power analysis with a defined measurement boundary and averaging interval, evaluate thermal feasibility under the package's heat-removal conditions, and close static timing and dynamic IR-drop analyses for its timing and power-delivery obligations. Because the public end-to-end demonstration examined in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect addresses a smaller processor problem, it leaves open whether this XRBench prompt can be carried through to a checked result.

**Outcome.** An AI-native design system earns adoption only when its candidates satisfy verified silicon constraints and, against a credible conventional alternative, either improve the result, reduce the total engineering cost of reaching a comparable result, or both, rather than merely chaining a generator to an EDA tool or producing a novel design description.
:::

Across all three layers, the practical test is whether the chosen assistance helped the team answer its architecture question with the required checks intact and an honest accounting of the total work. A focused local tool can pass that test on a bounded task without carrying the complete Lighthouse workflow, whereas a broader design system has to demonstrate the extra capability that its cross-layer coordination is meant to provide. In every case, the human architect remains responsible for interpreting the comparison and deciding what further work or signoff review the result warrants.

\FloatBarrier

## Open Questions

The pressures traced in this chapter show why architectural progress so often stalls on data movement, offload overhead, physical layout, or verification capacity rather than on how quickly a team can draft new designs. Turning that diagnosis into reliable automation raises five open research questions across computer architecture, electronic design automation, and machine learning:

- **When a model can generate thousands of candidate designs a day, how do we decide which ones are worth running through slow simulators and verification tools?** Making it cheap to draft RTL modules or compiler schedules creates a Jevons paradox: instead of saving time, a fast generator can flood cycle-accurate simulators, place-and-route licenses, and human reviewers with more designs than they can evaluate. Because some candidates simulate in seconds while others tie up tools and verification engineers for days, fixed batch sizes either leave expensive tools idle or create multi-day backlogs. We still lack good ways to weigh how much a candidate design will teach us against how long it will take to simulate and verify.

- **How can fast early-stage models catch hidden physical bottlenecks when a search tool steps outside a familiar hardware template?** Analytical models and learned surrogates can score millions of loop mappings or datapath configurations per hour, but they only know the wire delays, SRAM banking rules, and switching patterns of the templates they were calibrated on. Just as an unconstrained aerodynamic or structural optimizer will exploit a coarse mesh to propose shapes that cannot be manufactured, a hardware generator that steps outside a familiar template can cut local arithmetic energy while quietly triggering off-chip memory traffic, routing congestion, or inductive $L\frac{di}{dt}$ voltage droops that flip the rankings at signoff. Finding cheap physical checks or uncertainty signals that warn us before we spend days on place-and-route is a central challenge for multi-stage search.

- **Can we estimate how hard a candidate will be to verify before we write its RTL?** A clever cache-coherence shortcut or asynchronous interface may look great in a performance simulator while multiplying corner-case states, clock-domain crossings, and formal proof obligations far beyond a team's verification budget. Most design-space exploration tools optimize PPA as if verification were a fixed downstream tax, even though verification consumes the majority of engineering effort on leading-node chips. We need structural complexity metrics that predict early on whether a design will bog down model checkers and simulation coverage, so search tools can penalize designs that are fast on paper but intractable to verify.

- **How do we weigh peak efficiency today against the flexibility to handle tomorrow's workloads?** Hardwiring a fixed dataflow, scratchpad size, or number format maximizes performance per watt on today's benchmarks, but risks falling below the LogCA break-even granularity $g^*$ or operational-intensity threshold $\mathrm{OI}^*$ as soon as models shift toward sparse mixture-of-experts routing or paged key-value caches. Keeping programmable vector units, flexible interconnects, or spare on-chip SRAM buys insurance over a multi-year chip lifecycle at an immediate cost in die area and leakage power, much as power-grid planners pay upfront for flexible capacity when future demand is uncertain. We still lack co-design methods that can balance present efficiency against realistic shifts in future workloads and compiler schedules.

- **How can automated tools safely combine encrypted third-party IP blocks and multi-vendor chiplets without seeing their internal circuits?** Modern SoC and chiplet teams routinely integrate commercial processors, memory controllers, and UCIe die-to-die links delivered as fixed hard macros or encrypted RTL whose internal queues, power states, and clock-domain crossings are hidden. Standard pin protocols define basic handshakes, yet undocumented buffer limits or thermal coupling across die boundaries can still trigger deadlocks or tail-latency spikes under bursty traffic. Developing black-box probing techniques and interface contracts that guarantee end-to-end latency, power delivery, and deadlock freedom without exposing proprietary netlists would open multi-vendor systems to automated exploration.

## Summary

Architectural gains increasingly depend on how microarchitecture, specialization, software, and physical layout work together. The examples in this chapter make those couplings concrete: a faster arithmetic block can lose its advantage to offload overhead, a wider vector grouping can trigger register spills, and lower compute energy can be wiped out by off-chip memory traffic. Any useful comparison has to include the cross-layer interactions that can flip which design wins.

Exploring those trade-offs takes implementation effort, simulation time, and verification capacity. A large design space does not automatically make a study expensive, and an expensive study does not automatically call for AI. Where automation helps depends on which bottleneck is actually holding up the next engineering decision, what alternatives a tool makes practical to test, and what it costs to get an answer the team can trust. An AI-native design system makes sense when the current hardware template rules out better designs, though its value still has to be proved in practice.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Follow the full cost of a local speedup.** Include data movement, control, software overhead, and physical layout effects before treating a block-level gain as a system gain.
- **Evaluate hardware together with its software.** Compiler mappings, runtime behavior, and workload shifts can change which hardware organization wins.
- **Pick the modeling boundary that answers the question.** Include the cross-layer interactions that can flip the decision, using the simplest abstraction that captures them at each scale.
- **Budget for evaluation and verification, not just generation.** Candidate counts, simulation runtime, verification effort, and engineering cost are distinct bottlenecks, and tests, surrogates, and formal proofs establish different things.
- **Aim assistance at the real bottleneck and measure the whole workflow.** Use the simplest method the problem needs, including conventional automation, and count setup, simulation, and review time alongside the task that became faster.
:::

Once a team knows which bottleneck is delaying its next decision, it needs a disciplined way to organize the study around that bottleneck. A simulator number has to stay tied to the exact workload and candidate it measured, and a failed check has to inform the next design step. Those obligations fit together across a six-stage life cycle (Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit) that connects the initial architecture question to candidate generation, tool execution, evidence checks, and the final engineering decision (@sec-architecture-20-ontology).
